prose: I remember reading about Giant Spider being among the best green commons back in the days of the M10 and M12 core sets. Even more recently I gawked at the printing of Magnigoth Sentry , a strict upgrade on the existing formula. Now, we have Primordial Pachyderm , an upgrade further still. Four-drop green commons haven’t been too good as of late, but this one looks like it has enough going for it to earn a spot in most of your green decks.

name: Ragamuffin Raptor
prose: This is one of the best common 5-drops I’ve seen for a long time. Not only is Ragamuffin Raptor just a big Gravedigger , which is already an excellent start, but given the quality of some of the pizza cards in this set, getting one of them back almost sounds just as good.

name: Rocksteady, Crash Courser
prose: Unlike its boar counterpart, Rocksteady, Crash Courser is actually quite decent on its own. A 7/7 that can’t be blocked by multiple creatures is kind of annoying to have to deal with, plus you can forestcycle it.

name: Saved by the Shell
prose: Unlike some of the similar protection spells we’ve seen in the past, Saved by the Shell kind of does it all. Hexproof protects from most removal and indestructible protects from the rest. Plus, the +1/+1 counter combined with indestructible makes it an effective combat trick. I don’t normally like these cards, but this one literally does it all.

name: Tenderize
prose: There’s absolutely nothing wrong with a card like Tenderize . Two mana, instant, bite spell . Just good, clean removal for green , and every green deck will be happy to see it.

name: Transdimensional Bovine
prose: This is one hell of a weird creature… I mean, can a Transdimensional Bovine really fly? I guess that’s a question for someone who knows the lore of TMNT. But yeah, while 3 mana is a lot for a mana dork, ramping you an extra 2 mana is really strong, plus the 4 toughness allows you to block a good amount of early aggression.

name: Turtle Power!
prose: I’d have expected Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles to have a lot more turtles in it, but it seems that there are very few beyond the four main turtles themselves, and most of them are at higher rarities. There are also no black ones. A +2/+2 Glorious Anthem is definitely something to be excited about, but the lack of turtles makes me think that Turtle Power! won’t quite be enough to get the job done.

name: Venus, Torn Between Worlds
prose: The issue with Venus, Torn Between Worlds is that it’s just too big and expensive. You’re not likely to be able to play it on a turn when you also have spare blue mana to get a hit in with something else and draw a card. On future turns, your opponent will be more prepared for the impending onslaught. This just feels a little too situational to be a powerhouse, but there’s potential.

name: West Wind Avatar
prose: While I appreciate that only being able to sacrifice a land or a token is quite restrictive, the reward of 3 life right away and an extra card drawn in the end step is well worth it. All that attached to a 7-mana 7/7 with trample makes West Wind Avatar my dream ramp payoff , and you could even draw extra cards if you can enable disappear on future turns!

name: Zoo Escapees
prose: Two-mana 2/2s with upsides are always nice to see. The Mutagen tokens look like they’ll be quite valuable, so even if you need to trade off Zoo Escapees first, you do get nicely rewarded.

name: Baxter Stockman
prose: A 3/3 plus a 1/1 would be great if it cost 3 or even 4 mana, but for 5 mana it’s not great. Baxter Stockman ’s other ability can be relevant as soon as you play it, which makes it rather hard for your opponent to block your attacks each turn. It’s quite vulnerable to removal, though. A 3/3 is fairly easy to deal with, and this scientist won’t leave you too much value if that happens.

name: Bebop & Rocksteady
prose: Unlike many other similar overstatted creatures with downsides, Bebop & Rocksteady doesn’t require any kind of cost to just keep it around and do nothing. If you don’t have anything to sacrifice right away, you can comfortably wait until you do. In some decks, getting to sacrifice a permanent for no mana cost is going to be an upside that enables disappear abilities or whatever else you might find.

name: Brilliance Unleashed
prose: Brilliance Unleashed does say you can “choose one or both”, but that’s just to be a little more flexible. You really want to choose both. If you do, you get an easy two-for-one swing by killing a creature and reanimating another one. Six mana is a little on the expensive side, but the power is very much there to justify the cost.

name: Dark Leo & Shredder
prose: Giving all attacking ninjas deathtouch is a nasty ability. On the turn you sneak in Dark Leo & Shredder , it could be a ridiculous combat trick, especially if your opponent took the time to line up blocks on, for example, some 1/1 ninja tokens. The deathtouch also applies to itself, so it’s incredibly difficult to want to block Dark Leo & Shredder on future turns. Get one hit in and your new 1/1 deathtouch token will easily enable future sneak abilities, too. There’s a lot to like here, and it’s nice to see this ninja deck coming together.

name: Don & Leo, Problem Solvers
prose: There are some pretty great enters triggers in this set, but if you don’t have one, Don & Leo, Problem Solvers is little better than just a big vanilla creature. It deserve a second look if you have the right abilities to pair with it, but most decks won’t need this card.

name: Don & Raph, Hard Science
prose: Giving affinity for artifacts to the next spell you cast sounds incredible, but restricting it to noncreature spells really doesn’t bode well. Most decks aren’t likely to have that many noncreature spells in the first place, let alone any that really need to be discounted. Don & Raph, Hard Science is very specific, and I could definitely see it being powerful if it discounts a card like Brilliance Unleashed , but most decks aren’t going to be too bothered by this card at all.

name: EPF Point Squad
prose: This card kind of reminds me of Quandrix Pledgemage , which overperformed back in Strixhaven: School of Mages due to how frequently you could trigger it. EPF Point Squad isn’t anywhere near as good, but the better your alliance deck is, the better this card becomes because you’ll be able to trigger it a lot more often.

name: Foot Elite
prose: Giving an attacking creature +1/+0 and indestructible is a good ability, but the only thing that Foot Elite has to protect itself is its 4 points of toughness, which really isn’t enough to get the job done. This doesn’t look very impressive to me, though it’s a more flexible version of Hardened Escort , which was decent in Duskmourn .

name: Foot Ninjas
prose: While a little bit on the expensive side, Foot Ninjas is well worth the sneak cost. Hitting for 5 damage right away while gaining 3 life is a pretty huge life swing, which could be crucial if you’re trying to win a damage race.

name: Genghis Frog
prose: Isn’t trample just a weird ability to see on a 1/3 creature? I get that you can load Genghis Frog up with your Mutagen tokens, but that’s still weird to see. Anyway, free Mutagen tokens for every mutant creature you play, many of which also give you Mutagens themselves. This should rack up a bunch of these tokens, and you can then choose where all your extra +1/+1 counters are going to go. This is a pretty good home for them, too!

name: Go Ninja Go
prose: Go Ninja Go is a perfectly serviceable removal spell, even though a bite spell is typically better suited to green decks. The flicker mode that you can add to this is a really nice touch; even without a good option for it, you can just flicker something random and trigger your alliance abilities in the process.

name: Ice Cream Kitty
prose: This world really does have some bizarre creations in it…. Given the abundance of Mutagen tokens spread throughout this set, using Ice Cream Kitty to turn them into extra cards sounds pretty good to me. What stands out to me about this card is just how cheap it is. We’ve seen cards like this in several sets in the past, but they usually cost about 3 or 4 mana, and the ability costs a little more, too. At 2 to cast and 2 to activate, this looks like a really good common for the TMT Limited format.

name: Karai, Future of the Foot
prose: We’ve seen so many ways to enable the ninjas deck so far, which of course tells me that Karai, Future of the Foot ’s sneak cost is going to be very easy to enable. Reanimating just about any creature with its first hit is going to be a huge swing in both tempo and card advantage. Karai doesn’t even need to hit again, but the fact that it can keep going and give you a free Raise Dead every time you connect is just absurd. This is a great build-around for the deck, second perhaps only to…

name: Karai's Technique
prose: One of the most brutal combat tricks ever created was Consume Strength from back in Apocalypse . Getting to kill one creature while also letting one of yours kill another in combat is absolutely huge. In fact, it’s so powerful that very few similar effects have ever been printed since. Granted, Karai's Technique is only an instant if you cast it for its sneak cost, but that’s well worth setting up given the tremendous upside that you get. Even if you can’t do that, -3/-3 at sorcery speed can kill a lot of creatures in a pinch. This all adds up to what looks like one of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles ’ strongest nonrare cards.

name: Krang & Shredder
prose: If you have disappear enabled, Krang & Shredder immediately casts the top spell of your opponent’s deck for free. While the card you get is completely random, just about anything makes that worth it. After that, attacking and enabling disappear in the same turn sounds kind of hard to do, but you don’t need this duo to do much beyond that first turn to be great. Anything else you get is just a bonus.

name: The Last Ronin
prose: The Last Ronin is a highly acclaimed comic series from just a few years ago where Michelangelo is the last surviving turtle in an alternative future, seeking revenge for his fallen brothers. This card is also no joke. Board wipes are already good in Limited, but this one guarantees you a follow-up play on the next turn, followed by a huge lifelink swing on the one after that. This is very reminiscent of The Rise of Sozin , one of the best cards in Avatar ’s Draft format , and this might even be better.

name: Lessons from Life
prose: This is yet another Magic precedent. To my knowledge, Lessons from Life is the first card artwork outside of an Un-set or a special promo to feature actual Magic cards in it. I know that’ll annoy some people, but I came from a Yu-Gi-Oh! background, and this was a common feature in that game. Anyway, this card is great. Concentrate plus an extra land drop is awesome.

name: Mechanized Ninja Cavalry
prose: Time and time again, we’ve seen that two 1/1s for 2 mana is a great deal. Mechanized Ninja Cavalry ups the ante: Both of its creatures are artifacts, it’s a good creature to return for sneak costs, it has a flexible mana cost, and it’s also good for alliance triggers. All nice upsides that make me think this’ll be a premium common.

name: Mikey & Don, Party Planners
prose: You only need to cast one free spell off Mikey & Don, Party Planners to have made casting it worthwhile. About 61% of TMT’s creatures are mutants, ninjas, and/or turtles, so the right deck should have plenty of good hits in it. The main issue I see here is that a 4-mana 3/3 with ward 2 is pretty weak, so sometimes you’ll play Mikey & Don and it just won’t do anything relevant in the game.

name: Mikey & Leo, Chaos & Order
prose: With Mutagen tokens scattered throughout the set, Mikey & Leo, Chaos & Order has a ton of opportunities to trigger. Turning each Mutagen token into not just a counter but a free card is a great ability, and it’s even better that the ability appears on a 2-drop.

name: Mouser Mark III
prose: If you’re in blue/red, I’d say the odds that you control another artifact are pretty high. In other color combinations, there are Mutagen tokens and other such cards that make it so that Mouser Mark III ’s pesky downside shouldn’t get in your way very often. If that’s the case, this is a pretty solid 2-drop.

name: The Neutrinos
prose: This is a very weird and unique ability. Thanks to flickering a creature on attack, The Neutrinos should usually be at least a 3/4 flier, but it’ll often be quite a bit bigger than that. The funny thing you can do with this is to flicker a creature that you just played, effectively giving it haste . There are a lot of great targets for an ability like this, and when it comes with an oversized flier attached, I’m all in for it.

name: Nobody
prose: This is such a weird ability. The bare minimum is that this is a 3/2 plus a scry 1 for 3 mana, which isn’t bad by any means. But you can also return an artifact you control to your hand? This isn’t much of an upside. While you get to reuse that card’s enters the battlefield ability, you still have to pay its cost again, which often you just won’t want to do. Nobody isn’t even oversized for your trouble. This is fine, but it’s a very weird design.

name: North Wind Avatar
prose: In case you’re unaware, “a card you own from outside the game” means a card that’s in your sideboard . In Limited, that’s anything in your card pool that’s not in your main deck. So, is this any good? After all, is getting a card that wasn’t good enough to make the cut in your main deck even worth it? In this day and age, it definitely is. Your sideboard is likely to have all sorts of powerful cards that are simply too expensive or situational to include in your main, but grabbing them at will is going to be very useful. Besides, North Wind Avatar is still a huge 5/5 flier, and it draws you a spell when you play it, which is a great deal no matter what you get.

name: Pizza Face, Gastromancer
prose: This card is pretty funny, I really like it. I’ve said this a lot, but if you’ve been able to enable disappear before you play it, Pizza Face, Gastromancer immediately gives you a 2/4 plus a 3/3 for just 5 mana, which is excellent. The black/green deck in particular should be pretty good at enabling this turn after turn, and you just get to keep cranking out the +1/+1 counters. The 10-mana ability at the end is funny, essentially saying that this is the equivalent of five foods, but it’s basically never going to happen.

name: Punk Frogs
prose: This looks like a quintessential unplayable to me. Ward 3 is quite good, but Punk Frogs is a somewhat undersized vanilla creature otherwise. I think you’ll choose not to run this most of the time.

name: Putrid Pals
prose: Given that Putrid Pals has deathtouch, you don’t even need to have enabled disappear for it to have an impact on the board, though it’s obviously preferable. This is just a big vanilla creature at the end of the day, but a 5/5 deathtoucher is annoyingly hard to kill in combat because it trades with everything in a double or triple block scenario.

name: Raph & Leo, Sibling Rivals
prose: Most additional combat effects are expensive, clunky, or far too situational for your average game of Limited. Raph & Leo, Sibling Rivals is none of that, which makes me wonder if this is finally the card that’ll make it worthwhile. We’ve seen Fear of Missing Out do some good work in the Duskmourn Limited format, so I imagine Raph & Leo will do so too.

name: Raph & Mikey, Troublemakers
prose: I think I’ve found my next commander to build around. In Limited, Raph & Mikey, Troublemakers is already problematic as a 7/7 with haste and trample. It hits hard and fast, and it tops your curve incredibly well. The free creature you get when it attacks is completely random, so you don’t know if it’ll matter or not, but anything for free is a good thing. If you happen to hit something expensive, you’re absolutely set.

name: Slithering Cryptid
prose: A 2/3 plus a Mutagen token for 3 mana is very similar to a 3/4 for 4, but it should be so much better than that. The Mutagen tokens look quite valuable, so I’m sure Slithering Cryptid will be a decent common.

name: Splinter, Radical Rat
prose: Splinter, Radical Rat is clearly designed with Commander in mind as a 3-color commander that combines this set’s white/black ninjas with the traditionally blue (and black) ninjas from Kamigawa and other past sets. In Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles , we’re unlikely to want blue mana in our ninja decks, so we should probably discount that ability entirely. Still, a 3-drop that doubles our ninjas’ triggered abilities sounds fine, especially as they basically all have triggered abilities of some kind.

name: Tainted Treats
prose: I’m always happy with Putrefy in a Limited environment, so give me a functional reprint with a nice upside like Tainted Treats and we’re very much in business.

name: Tokka & Rahzar, Terrible Twos
prose: A 2-drop 3/2 with menace isn’t too bad, but Tokka & Rahzar, Terrible Twos kind of stops there. The damage ability is mostly irrelevant in this format, but it does punish many of the sneak spells, which makes this card pretty strong against ninja decks. This turtle wolf mutant will however be rather lacking when you play against other decks.

name: Chrome Dome
prose: I’m far more interested in Chrome Dome being a sort of typal lord for your artifact creatures than ever trying to activate its second ability. Five mana is a lot to spend to get a token that’s just going to die at the end of the turn, though at least it’s something you can sink your mana into when you reach the late game with nothing else to do.

name: Everything Pizza
prose: I don’t see any real reason to build a 5-color deck in this format, but Everything Pizza makes me hope that it could happen at least once. You can use this to fix your mana in a pinch, and the black/green deck could certainly use more things to sacrifice, so this should be somewhat playable even without all the colors to win the game with.

name: Henchbots
prose: Is that… a colorless Banisher Priest ? Seriously? I mean sure, it costs 4 mana and can only target a tapped creature, but Henchbots is still an extremely powerful effect for any deck to have access to.

name: Krang, Utrom Warlord
prose: Six or 7 mana is reasonable to expect to cast, and even 8 is possible if you put a bit of effort into it, or a format is slow enough. Nine feels like a step too far. Krang, Utrom Warlord is obviously powerful if you can land it, but doing so looks like an insurmountable task to me.

name: Omni-Cheese Pizza
prose: If your deck likes having artifacts on the battlefield, you could certainly do worse than an Omni-Cheese Pizza or two. They immediately replace themselves with a fresh card and then help to fix your mana a little. They gain life as all foods do, or you can find some other way to use them depending on your deck.

name: The Ooze
prose: Given that there are usually at least a few cards in the graveyards, The Ooze can create a Mutagen token nearly every turn cycle of the game, plus more when your creatures die. This enables you to pile all your counters onto one creature, then when it dies, you get a bunch of Mutagens and can pile them all onto something else. This card is pretty sweet, and there are a few decks in the TMT Limited format that will use it very well.

name: Skateboard
prose: I suppose they made this very generic so it can be reprinted in the inevitable future Universes Beyond set for The Simpsons . Well, I hope not, because Skateboard looks incredibly mediocre to me. Haste is a very powerful ability to grant for only 1 mana, but spending a whole card on this just isn’t going to be worth it most of the time.

name: Technodrome
prose: Technodrome is an absolute house. Of course, you need to be a deck that can actually use it, since on its own it does literally nothing. More than likely it’ll be the green decks with an abundance of Food and Mutagen tokens that can use this the best, especially as the Mutagen tokens allow you to turbo this up to a 6/6 and start getting into combat. Even if you’re not attacking, getting to turn a token into an extra card each turn is quite a powerful ability, especially when it doesn’t cost any mana to use.

name: Turtle Blimp
prose: “Oh my god! How can you afford these things!” -Joe Swanson, Family Guy Vehicles kind of suck, but Turtle Blimp giving you a 2/2 token that can then be used to crew it does make it worth playing. Besides, flying creatures are always valuable and crew 2 is a pretty accessible cost to enable it.

name: Turtle Van
prose: A 4/4 vehicle with just crew 1 is a little above average these days, but vehicles need to do a lot more to be worth a slot in our decks. Turtle Van churns out a lot of +1/+1 counters if it gets to attack, though it’s somewhat easy to disrupt. Your opponent has a few opportunities available to deal with this before you get a trigger from it. That said, getting one, two, or even more counters with this ability is huge, which really incentivizes you to pick your moments and make sure it can’t be dealt with.

name: Weather Maker
prose: Three-drop mana rocks range from unplayable to pretty good, all based on the extra abilities they may have. Weather Maker is pretty unique in that it can accelerate mana even further with its two counters ability, but notably also kill creatures with the last ability. Most mana rocks aren’t capable of also being removal, which I think makes this quite decent.

name: TCRI Building
prose: Gain lands are fantastic to see in any set. Most of the decks we play in this format will be one of these combinations, so if you see a land for your deck, you should probably take it over most medium commons and shore up your mana base, but you also don’t need to prioritize them over very good cards.

name: Escape Tunnel
prose: Escape Tunnel is a cool reprint to see, too. It’s functionally the same as Evolving Wilds but with a little extra bonus, and you were already happy with Evolving Wilds in the first place. As with the gain lands, take it over medium commons, but don’t pass over better cards for it.

name: Northampton Farm
prose: This is very reminiscent of Endless Sands , a land which looked incredible at first, but proved to be virtually unplayable. Northampton Farm is a much better deal in terms of mana, but the cost of putting a colorless land into your deck likely far outweighs the niche potential that this card has.

name: Turtle Lair
prose: Rogue's Passage is a nasty little land that can win some board stalls here and there but is also a liability in your mana base since it’s a colorless land. Turtle Lair is quite a bit better than that, as it’ll sometimes tap for colored mana and help to cast your spells on time, then later make it so that you can close out a game. It’s not broken or anything, but it’s a very nice addition to the right decks.

name: Path to Exile
prose: A lot of IPs feature stories where a protagonist ends up alone, exiled from their friends and/or family, and has to figure out how to overcome their troubles. As such, if WotC continues to do source material bonus sheets for Universes Beyond sets, we’ll keep seeing Path to Exile over and over. Not that I’m complaining, because it’s an excellent removal spell and you should always take it and play it.

name: Brainstorm
prose: Brainstorm might not be good enough to talk about, but it’s such a classic that I can’t help it. One-mana cantrips have a tendency to be bad unless you have a reason to cast lots of spells. Without a good reason in TMT, it’s possible that you’ll never play Brainstorm. Still, it’s very good when you can use a landcycler to shuffle your library , so maybe there’s something to consider there.

name: Cytoplast Manipulator
prose: We’ve seen just how many +1/+1 counters are scattered throughout this set, which potentially makes Cytoplast Manipulator the strongest creature on the board. You can steal just about anything and use its own graft ability to put a counter onto something that wouldn’t otherwise get one. The obvious downside is how vulnerable this is to removal, and you’ll give back the creatures you stole when it dies, but if you can protect it somehow then this’ll dominate a game.

name: Arcbound Ravager
prose: Arcbound Ravager is quite an unassuming card, but an extremely powerful one. The ability to sacrifice any artifact for free and whenever you like shouldn’t be underestimated, and the modular ability lets you turn all of your artifacts into one very large creature, whether that’s the Ravager itself or something with some better abilities. This is a card that has been synonymous with the affinity archetype for decades, and it’s bound to have some kind of impact in Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles .

name: Conqueror's Flail
prose: The power and toughness boost you can get from Conqueror's Flail is usually capped at +2/+2, but thanks to the hybrid cards in this set, it’s not unreasonable to see that climb on certain boards. Similarly, it could also drop to just +1/+1. What’s really interesting is the Grand Abolisher -esque ability that allows you to attack without fear of running into a combat trick or removal spell. All of that is fine, though this is still an equipment, which typically needs to do a bit more to be considered good.

name: Metallic Mimic
prose: If you have a lot of one creature type in your deck, which in TMT is likely to be either ninjas or mutants, then Metallic Mimic is going to slot right in. It’s awkward to draw this late, but the reverse scenario makes up for it: How powerful will it be if you get to play this on turn 2 and have most of your creatures be that much bigger for the trouble?

name: Shadowspear
prose: The key to Shadowspear is the cheap cost for granting lifelink to any creature you play. Lifelink is one of the most powerful abilities in Limited, which makes this a very valuable equipment to have around. The +1/+1 and trample isn’t too bad, either.

name: Sword of Sinew and Steel
prose: It’s really quite funny to see this card here given that WotC have made functional reprints of existing cards just to remove references to planeswalkers , yet Sword of Sinew and Steel literally says “ destroy target planeswalker ”. The best part of this card is that it grants protection from red and black , the two strongest removal colors. Destroying an artifact is also a nice bonus, but we were already sold before we got to that.

name: Umezawa's Jitte
prose: Okay then, let’s talk about Umezawa's Jitte . This card is the single most broken Limited card in the history of this game. If you’ve never played with or against it, then it might be hard to appreciate just how powerful it is, but let me assure you that the rating I’ve given it is accurate. First of all, it’s colorless, so it goes in literally every deck. It’s cheap to cast and to equip. It only requires the equipped creature to have dealt damage. Not damage to a player, just damage. Your opponent blocks? That’s fine, Jitte still charges itself. You can use those counters to make your creature too big to block effectively, at which point it would charge again, or just to kill creatures on the board. If your opponent can destroy it, you can just cash them in for some life. Still unsure? I don’t blame you. When I first saw this card some 16 years ago, I smirked at it. Then I played it for

name: Undercity Sewers
prose: Blue/black isn’t a supported color combination in this format, but Undercity Sewers can still be useful as a surveil land or to fix for a splash . Plus, it’s an expensive card, so you’ll probably take it for cash value.

name: 70,000 Light-Years from Home
prose: The plot of Star Trek: Voyager involves the fledgling crew of the U.S.S. Voyager as they end up on the other side of the galaxy, 70,000 Light-Years from Home . So yeah, exiling a creature or spacecraft is a pretty resonant ability for this card to have. It’s basically a much weaker Path to Exile , but Path is so powerful already that that’s hardly a bad thing. You probably won’t want to play this early, but exiling a big creature in the late game so efficiently should be great.

name: Andromedan Automatons
prose: This is going to be a really fun challenge during a booster draft. The first copy of Andromedan Automatons is basically unplayable, but once you find a second one, the first one you play draws you a spell when it enters. That’s pretty good, and if you find a third or even a fourth copy, they get even better.

name: Antagonist Incorporator
prose: Antagonist Incorporator looks like a great way to swarm the board with additional Borg tokens. Your Borg decks already want to go wide, and not only does this help you to do that, but it also rewards you for it. Plus, the tokens you make also have this ability and can create even more tokens. The only thing that could hold this back is that you need to connect with your creatures to get them to trigger, and that might not always be possible, but this feels like an incredibly powerful card if you can enable it.

name: Assembly Specialist
prose: Two mana for a pair of 1/1s is always a good deal when we get it. When you add in the fact that the Borg want to be a go-wide aggro deck centered around artifact creatures , Assembly Specialist looks like one of the best ways to start your curve in that deck. I’d prioritize this very early when drafting a Borg deck. It’s less good but still solid in other white decks.

name: Brad Boimler, Eager Ensign
prose: Brad Boimler, Eager Ensign is one of the main characters from one of the animated series, Lower Decks . While I’m not very familiar with the show, this card is extremely good. A 2/2 lifelinker for 2 mana is a great start, but Boimler pulls a bit of double duty by being a great build-around for both white/blue spacecraft and white/green counters. You can use it to quickly station a spacecraft or just get extra utility from your various doctor creatures, and both sound pretty good.

name: Captain Benjamin Sisko
prose: The badass captain of Deep Space Nine , Captain Benjamin Sisko functions kind of like a Hero of Precinct One but for dilemmas. I’ll happily take that. There are so many modal spells and abilities in Star Trek that this seems like a great card to take early and build around. I don’t think we’re likely to use Sisko’s 5-color activated ability , but it’s still very good without it.

name: Captain Jean-Luc Picard
prose: Here, we have the best Captain in the whole show (fight me), Captain Jean-Luc Picard . Legendary actor Patrick Stewart brought this incredible character to life through 10 TV seasons (across TNG and Picard) and four movies, and he is one of my reasons for loving this show in the first place. Picard’s greatest strength as a captain was in the way he inspired and mentored his crew, so of course the card gives +1/+1 to your whole team and creates more officers whenever you cast creatures or spacecraft. I don’t think you’re very likely to search for any spacecraft with its final ability, but I love this card regardless.

name: Command Decision
prose: This looks eerily similar to Surgical Precision , which we just saw in Reality Fracture . Command Decision is a decent removal spell, but one that’s quite situational and might not find a target. Granted, you can cast it to draw a card when that happens, but I’m not in the habit of casting 2-mana cantrips if I can help it.

name: Command Subadjunct
prose: Vigilance carries a lot of extra weight in this set as it can allow you to attack with your creatures and then station a spacecraft with them afterwards. Even so, Command Subadjunct feels like it’s only slightly better than a vanilla 2/1 for 1, which is very playable, but nothing exciting.

name: Conquest Mission
prose: While taking a turn off to play Conquest Mission doesn’t sound too appealing, giving you a free 1/1 every single time you play an artifact sounds absolutely incredible. This clearly rewards you for building your deck to maximize it by filling it with as many artifacts as you can find. Knowing that the Borg power each other up just means that a black/white deck with this card will be able to get even more value out of it. This is a build-around that I’m very excited to play with, and I hope it works.

name: Deanna Troi, Psychic Counsel
prose: Deanna Troi, Psychic Counsel in TNG is one of the things that made the show look so ahead of its time, and the card is quite good. Troi’s very good when you cast it early and a lot of your creatures enter with counters, and less good the later you play it. On balance, that makes this card pretty good in most creature-heavy white decks.

name: DOT-7 Repair Squad
prose: Untapping a creature for 2 mana and only at sorcery speed sounds kind of useless to me, but it can be helpful if you want to station a spacecraft. Aside from that, DOT-7 Repair Squad doesn’t look very good at all and will probably be quite bad. That said, I thought the same about Wakandan Drone Flock , and that ended up being very good within the context of Marvel Super Heroes , so you never know.

name: Dr. Beverly Crusher
prose: An old friend of Captain Picard’s, Dr. Beverly Crusher was the heart of the Enterprise crew for six of the seven seasons of TNG. She was more than just the ship’s doctor; she was often the moral compass that Picard would turn to in his darkest moments. Here, this doctor is an Ajani's Pridemate that also doubles lifegain triggers, so it picks up two +1/+1 counters every time you gain life. That sounds good, but with no lifegain theme to back it up, Dr. Beverly Crusher doesn’t look that good. There are a lot of random lifegain sources, so it should do some work in the right deck, but Star Trek isn’t set up for this card at all.

name: Dr. McCoy, Surly Surgeon
prose: I could easily be wrong here, but this kind of effect doesn’t seem very good in the first place and even less good on a creature with such weak stats. It does make it very difficult for your opponent to get into combat with some of your creatures, but unless yours are already big enough, that doesn’t even amount to much. At 3 mana, Dr. McCoy, Surly Surgeon would be efficient enough to take notice of, but at 4 it just seems over-costed and too weak.

name: Emergency Medical Hologram
prose: Emergency Medical Hologram is such an unassuming 1-drop that I think it might actually be good enough. Putting its +1/+1 counter on itself isn’t the best play you could make, as a 1/2 on the board is very weak. However, putting it on just about any other creature later in the game is bound to be annoying, especially if it helps a creature attack into opposing blockers. It’s also an artifact creature for the Borg decks, which is bound to be relevant.

name: Excalbian Gamemaster
prose: Okay, this is just absurd. Excalbian Gamemaster is the quintessential “army-in-a-can” creature, giving you a minimum of two 1/1s when it enters and probably a lot more than that if you’ve built around it. It’s even very splashable so that no matter what, if you’re a deck built around strange new worlds, you’ll be able to play this. I wouldn’t be surprised if this was the best card in Star Trek Limited.

name: Federation Field Medic
prose: You had me at “draw a card”. I sincerely hope to always be able to draw a card off of Federation Field Medic . But if we can’t, it’s still pretty good to play it as a 3/2 plus a +1/+1 counter, so this is just a great card for the +1/+1 counters deck.

name: Federation Resupply
prose: A one-off conditional tutor spell isn’t worth spending your mana on, even if what you search for is really powerful. However, Federation Resupply lets you search for two things overall, kind of like a white Mystical Teachings . Is that good enough? I could definitely see running it in a deck that had several things to search for, but most of time this is going to be far too weak.

name: Free Borg Revolutionaries
prose: As we’ve seen the last few sets, basic landcycling is a very powerful ability, no matter how bad the creature you put it on happens to be. Free Borg Revolutionaries also happens to be quite a powerful creature when you play it. +1/+1 to your whole team is very good in the right spot, and a 4/5 for 5 mana isn’t the worst when you consider that the landcycling is the main reason to play it.

name: Ghost of Illyria
prose: There are a lot of good enters triggers in Star Trek , so it shouldn’t be too hard for Ghost of Illyria to shine in. Most of the spacecraft also have triggers you can utilize, since this works with any nonland permanent. Sorcery-speed flicker effects aren’t usually that strong, but like any spell, attaching it to a creature with good stats changes that equation enormously.

name: Hologram Janeway
prose: I often talk about the effect of Luminarch Aspirant and how broken it is in Limited. Hologram Janeway has a remarkably similar effect, but with a lot of extra hoops to jump through. Those hoops don’t seem too prohibitive, so I could see this being a very good card in the red/white deck where it belongs, but also with black/white Borg and artifact creatures.

name: Malfunctioning Holodeck
prose: I love the flavor behind this card. In TNG, the Holodeck would frequently malfunction, trapping its users inside it until the problem could be resolved, so of course this is a Banishing Light variant. Malfunctioning Holodeck is your standard white removal for the set, but being an artifact should also help it to play well with TRK’s themes.

name: The Measure of a Man
prose: This iconic TNG episode is one of my favorites by far, but sadly the card version leaves much to be desired. The Measure of a Man would be great if you had a way to bounce or sacrifice it before the final ability goes off, but I don’t think TRK has much of that. Instead, this is mostly just a very slow flicker that comes with a free Clue token , which is far too situational for most decks.

name: Miles O'Brien, Transporter Ops
prose: Before Colm Meaney’s Miles O’Brien became the chief of operations on Deep Space Nine, he was the Transporter Chief aboard the Enterprise-D in The Next Generation . Whenever a story involved some sort of transporter malfunction, Chief O’Brien was there to pick up the pieces. As such, it’s very fitting that Miles O'Brien, Transporter Ops beams up a creature when it enters and then rewards you at the end of any turn in which you returned anything else to your hand). None of the archetypes in Star Trek are specifically centered around this mechanic, but Chief O’Brien is still a very good payoff for it and I’m sure the card will find a home somewhere.

name: The Needs of the Many
prose: In the climax of The Wrath of Khan , Spock sacrifices his own life to save the Enterprise crew from Khan’s final gambit. With his final, dying breath, he simply reminds Kirk that “ The Needs of the Many outweigh the needs of the few, or the one.” This card isn’t particularly good. Protecting your whole team isn’t a particularly desirable effect in Limited. Board wipes are pretty rare, and sacrificing a creature to use this effect isn’t good enough either. The card is incredibly thematic, but simply not good.

name: Oberth-Class Starship
prose: It may take a lot to station this little ship, but the fact that it immediately draws you a card (albeit, a basic Plains ) is the key takeaway here. Oberth-Class Starship is a very playable card in any white deck, and there are also some nice synergies to find with it.

name: Peace in Our Time
prose: This is a cool build-around that might be worth building around, but the idea of letting my opponent draw cards for free doesn’t really inspire me with confidence. Peace in Our Time just seems far too cute, especially against an opponent that could potentially find a removal spell for it before it gets up to 12 counters. I’ll be trying this alternate wincon for myself, but I recommend others stay away from it.

name: Pet Sehlat
prose: There is really not much difference between Pet Sehlat and a vanilla 3/3 with no downside, the latter of which wouldn’t be playable. Raging Kronch was still pretty good almost a decade ago, and this can turbo-station or hit you 8-power payoffs quickly, so it has merit even when it can’t attack. Plus, it can always block without restriction.

name: Picard, Leading by Example
prose: While effects like this one are best when you can use them at instant speed, the fact that Picard, Leading by Example starts out by giving +2/+2 means that it can turn just about any creature into a legitimate threat. Make this creature any bigger and now your 1/1s can attack as 4/4s or even 5/5s, pushing through enemy blockers. This ability also puts more power on the board for the red/white archetype, which might be a big help. Picard is a very aggressively-slanted creature, but white’s decks mostly look like they want to attack a lot, so it should be able to find a home in any of them.

name: Primary Unimatrix Adjunct
prose: Double strike is an extremely powerful ability, so giving it to your whole team should be pretty good. My main problem with Primary Unimatrix Adjunct is just how vulnerable it looks. It does seem like you’d need to protect it if you want any chance of it surviving, and having it die in the middle of combat puts your other creatures at risk.

name: Pure Energy
prose: I was a fan of Predictive Preparations in Reality Fracture , though it didn’t really perform well, but I’m not a fan of Pure Energy . The fact that you need three creatures in play to beam it up (one to beam up and the other two to target) really doesn’t inspire me with any hope. I’d leave this one in the sideboard for now.

name: Rutherford, Upgraded Ensign
prose: Getting to look at your top six cards means that if you’ve built your deck correctly, Rutherford, Upgraded Ensign will hit an artifact very often. Let’s say there are 10 artifacts left in your deck when you play Rutherford on turn 3. That gives you a 92.63% chance to find at least one artifact. I’ll take that deal any day.

name: Saavik, Stoic Student
prose: One could look at Saavik, Stoic Student and see a white Flametongue Kavu . While that may be the case, Saavik is far more situational and quite inefficient. It’s at least two creature types to put towards its federation ability, but if that’s all you have, 2 damage won’t do very much when you’re late enough in the game to cast a 5-drop. There will be plenty of times when Saavik is a great two-for-one play, but also many more when it’ll be stuck in your hand doing not much of anything.

name: Set Phasers to . . .
prose: Looks like we’ll have to Set Phasers to . . . kill most of the time. One mana for 3 damage is a very efficient rate for a removal spell, even if you can only use it in combat. And every now and again, picking stun will let you interact favorably with a bigger creature.

name: Shields Up!
prose: Just like Take Up the Shield before it, Shields Up! should be a highly effective combat trick that protects a creature against just about anything. While costing 2 mana isn’t ideal, hexproof and indestructible covers pretty much all your bases and makes it worth playing.

name: Shuttle Ace
prose: I don’t see Shuttle Ace being very playable. It’s a very replaceable 5-drop, and it gives very little value when you play it. It’s just very unexciting, and I think we can move on.

name: Sulu, Space Swashbuckler
prose: Oh my, indeed! The legendary George Takei brought Mr. Sulu to life, the pilot of the Starship Enterprise . Sulu, Space Swashbuckler recreates one of the character’s most iconic moments from the show with a heck of a lot of style ( editor’s note: Yes, we know that “Oh, my!” is a George Takei meme, not something Sulu ever said ). A 2/2 for 2 with first strike is already very annoying to deal with, but then any equipment or spacecraft you play will let Sulu draw you a free card, especially if you have a spacecraft to station. I expect Sulu to be a very solid build-around card, but you don’t even need to enable it very often to get some utility out of this pilot.

name: Tactical Officer
prose: As a 2-mana 2/1, Tactical Officer really needs to make use of its ability. Unfortunately, that ability isn’t even active until you have a board full of creatures, so I don’t think this is something you want to play unless you just really need a 2-drop .

name: Test of Conviction
prose: Symmetrical draw spells , even ones that aren’t entirely symmetrical, are never very good. As such, we’re really looking at Test of Conviction as a spell that distributes +1/+1 counters, which frankly isn’t very good either. I think this one is going to fall short of the mark, but if the counters deck really needs an effect like this, at least it’s here.

name: There's Coffee in that Nebula
prose: In only the fifth episode of Voyager , the crew find that their energy levels are critically low, meaning Janeway can’t use the replicators to make a good cup of coffee. They find a nearby nebula that they believe can provide them with a new power source, leading to Janeway’s immortal line: There's Coffee in that Nebula . As much as this is a meme (the episode wasn’t particularly good after all), the card itself looks quite strong, essentially like a white Think Twice with a bit of card selection thrown in.

name: Troubling Tribbles
prose: The tribbles are a weird creature in Star Trek lore that multiply exceedingly quickly. Troubling Tribbles does exactly that, but they’re next to useless when they do. After a few turns, if they aren’t dealt with, you might have four, eight, or even 16 of them, but they have 0 power and can’t block, so what good are they? If you can find a way to mass pump them, this card might actually be useful, but that’s not trivial to do. That said, I can’t wait to beat an opponent with an army of tribbles!

name: Una Chin-Riley, Number One
prose: This kind of effect isn’t bad in theory, but costing 5 mana is just far too much for Una Chin-Riley, Number One to be something I’m ever particularly happy to play. I’d assume that you can cast it and get a trigger from it on the same turn, but that’s by no means guaranteed, and a 4/5 isn’t the most interesting of stat lines if it isn’t getting to trigger.

name: U.S.S. Enterprise-A, Free Spirit
prose: The U.S.S. Enterprise-A, Free Spirit has to be one of the strongest spacecraft we’ve ever seen. It’s essentially a Baneslayer Angel that also creates three 1/1s on entering. It only requires six charge counters to become a creature, which the three 1/1s can provide over the course of two turns. Even if your opponent can deal with this spacecraft, you still got your free tokens, so it’s not even that bad for you. This is how you design iconic aspects of the show! The Enterprise is one of the most recognizable spacecraft in all of pop culture, and this being one of the strongest cards in TRK is exactly what we want to see.

name: U.S.S. Excelsior, Cutting Edge
prose: Destroying a tapped creature isn’t always going to be something you can do, but when you can, the U.S.S. Excelsior, Cutting Edge will be a strong two-for-one. While it will be hard to station, as long as you get to remove a creature, you don’t even need to do so right away. There are also a few ways to pick it back up and reuse the triggered ability , which makes it a very useful card if you can utilize it correctly.

name: Vexing Drone
prose: Tapping an opponent’s creature is a pretty nice ability to have in an aggressive deck, and Vexing Drone has the magic stats of a 2/2 for 2, meaning we’d probably play it regardless. This is a solid creature for the Borg decks that actually gets better later in the game.

name: Anthropological Mission
prose: Getting to draw a card whenever you play a noncreature spell could be quite powerful. The first two spells only let you loot , but every spell thereafter nets you a whole new card. Anthropological Mission requires a little bit of time to get going, but if you can give it that time, it should be very effective. Load up on beam me up spells if you’re going to build around it.

name: The Caretaker
prose: Facing dilemmas seems remarkably easy to do in Star Trek , and The Caretaker has got to be the best payoff for them. You can trigger it in every end step , so instant-speed modal spells might be able to add up to two triggers every turn cycle. The Caretaker may be a 6-drop, but a few free spells plus a 5/6 vigilance creature makes a huge impact in any game you’d play it in.

name: Cetacean Ops
prose: We’ve seen a few 3-mana 2/2s in recent sets that pick up a +1/+1 counter whenever you cast a noncreature spell, and they’ve all been bad. Cetacean Ops being a 4-mana 3/3 actually makes me less inclined to want to play it. If I had H.M.S. Bounty, Unlikely Timeship available, then I might be a little more interested, but it’s still not a very good card.

name: Cloak and Phaser
prose: Cloak and Phaser looks like an incredible payoff spell for strange new worlds. At 6 mana it’s very castable, but a little too expensive. At 5 or less it’s incredible. To accomplish this, you only need three or more different lands, which sounds very doable. In a good build of strange new worlds, the thought of getting to cast this for significantly less mana doesn’t seem all that unlikely either. This card is a very real incentive for this deck, and one I’m going to be very excited to build around for myself.

name: Cloistered Telepath
prose: I’m not quite sure where Cloistered Telepath will fit in this format, but decent triggered ability like this makes it a good option for beam me up spells. It’s quite weak though, so I think I’ll cut this more often than not.

name: Consider the Prime Directive
prose: Most conditional counterspells get significantly worse in the late game, as the more lands your opponent has, the fewer spells you’ll actually be able to counter. However, Consider the Prime Directive is never dead. Stunning a creature and drawing a  card is also a very good mode to have access to. This also causes you to face a dilemma, so it looks like it’ll be really good in the format.

name: Data, New Life
prose: I’ve been very wrong about cards like this in the past, so I’m being extra careful with how I rate Data, New Life . It naturally grows every turn just from you drawing your card for the turn, but you’ll really want to combine it with other sources of card draw to make Data really shine. I think that’ll be fine to do, but starting out as a 0/1 will surely hold it back.

name: Deep Space Scan
prose: If this format is as slow as I suspect it will be, Deep Space Scan could actually be very powerful. However, requiring at least four or five different lands and a slow enough format to accommodate it doesn’t sound like a winning combination to me. I’m sure this could be good in the right deck, but as I’ve said, I don’t think that’ll come up all too often.

name: Dominion Saboteur
prose: Five mana is a little on the expensive side for a Clone , but that really shouldn’t matter. These types of creatures are always fantastic, and Dominion Saboteur is no different. Not only can it copy any creature or artifact on the battlefield, but it also copies the counters on it, so you can also copy a fully stationed spacecraft. No matter what, this will always be the strongest creature on the battlefield once you play it, and it’ll be well worth taking early in a draft.

name: Emergency Holographic Crew
prose: Spacecraft don’t seem too likely to end up in the graveyard, since you need to station them before they can trade off in combat. That said, getting a sweet two-for-one with Emergency Holographic Crew is hard to pass up. It seems like most of the time you’d have to surveil with it, but hopefully you can wait long enough until you can get back your Suurok-Class Science Vessel or something similar.

name: Energize
prose: This card reminds me a lot of Silent Departure , a very powerful interactive spell in its own right. Like its predecessor, Energize , gives you two potentially powerful tempo spells. They may be sorceries , but resetting a spacecraft, removing an annoying blocker, or whatever else is well worth playing this card for.

name: Ensign Pavel Chekov
prose: This Ensign Pavel Chekov card has quite a unique design. It might be possible to mill out your opponent if you can combine it with other similar effects, but the most important part of Chekov’s effect is the ability to steal a land from your opponent. You’re very likely to find one out of the cards you exile, letting Chekov act as a defensive cantrip creature that advances your gameplan in the Strange New Worlds deck.

name: Enterprise NX-01
prose: The Enterprise NX-01 was the ship piloted by the crew from Star Trek: Enterprise . This card certainly has the potential to be powerful, but without knowing how fast the format will be, it’s difficult to evaluate. I certainly think being a spacecraft instead of just a creature holds it back a lot, but it’ll be best suited for some sort of tempo deck that can use it to get rid of a blocker and continue applying pressure to an opponent.

name: Federation Probe
prose: Say it with me: “We don’t underestimate 1-drops!” I’m very happy to play Federation Probe on turn 1 and get a surveil along with my flying 1/1, then later in the game it can buff a creature and potentially get a better attack in. But that’s not what makes this card special. It’s a dilemma, a cheap creature to beam up, and a cheap artifact. This looks really good, and my relatively high grade for a common might not even be high enough.

name: Guidance Failure
prose: So yeah, we’re back to this design again. Four mana for an instant that puts a target creature on the top or bottom of its owner’s deck. We’ve seen so many variations on Guidance Failure that we know it’s going to be good, especially with the cost reduction to help slot it into more places on the curve.

name: Gwyndala, the Progeny
prose: Gwyndala, the Progeny is a very simple card in Limited. It’s a 2/2 for 2 that leaves behind a very relevant equipment after it’s removed from the field. That’s definitely good, but not too exciting. There isn’t much equipment in Star Trek for its second ability to be of any use in Limited, so it really stops there. Blue decks should play Gwyndala, but they don’t need to go out of their way to pick it up.

name: Highly Illogical
prose: Four mana Cancel s aren’t where we typically want to be, but you can’t cast Cancel on turn 2 to hit a cheap spell. Highly Illogical actually seems like a pretty logical card to play in a blue deck, especially one based around noncreature spells.

name: H.M.S. Bounty, Unlikely Timeship
prose: In Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home , Kirk and the Enterprise crew travel back in time to rescue a pod of Humpback Whales and bring them to the 23rd century. The H.M.S. Bounty, Unlikely Timeship is the captured Klingon warbird that they use to do this, making this an incredible top-down design. There are two whale cards in Star Trek , one of which is the blue landcycler, so it should be relatively easy to find one or two to pair with this card. You get the upside right away by getting to tutor for one, and you might even be able to attack with it on the following turn as well as get the extra turn . A few things have to go right for all of this to work, but the payoff is certainly there to allow you to try.

name: Hoshi Sato, Exolinguist
prose: You don’t need any other creatures on the battlefield for Hoshi Sato, Exolinguist to be worth playing. It counts its own creature types, so you should always be able to look at two cards and pick the best one. If you do have other creatures, you get to look at potentially a lot more cards and cherry pick something very good. At the bare minimum, it’s a cantrip creature, assuming your opponent doesn’t remove this scientist before its trigger resolves, at best it’ll find you the best card in your deck while adding to the board.

name: Humpback Whales
prose: Humpback Whales is blue’s basic landcycler, which already makes it quite playable. A 5/6 vigilance creature with ward is certainly more than nothing should you end up casting it, but the fact that you can use Humpback Whales to fix your mana at any point you draw it makes this card extremely useful for any deck.

name: Interstellar Effigy
prose: Usually, we like our Man-o'-War s to be much cheaper than 5 mana, but Interstellar Effigy can still get the job done. It may come down later in the curve, but bouncing a creature while adding to your board is still very powerful. Also, it’s a common, when most cards like this tend to be uncommon, so we’ll see it far more often.

name: Jett Reno, Problem Solver
prose: Easily one of the best characters in Star Trek: Discovery , Jett Reno, Problem Solver is quite a nifty little build-around for the dilemmas deck. It’s hard to know how frequently you can trigger it, but I’d imagine that a good version of this deck can do so with relative ease. I doubt you’ll be able to get it to 4 power very often, not for a lack of ways to trigger it, but because it’ll take so long that an opponent will probably remove Reno before it happens. Still, there are other ways to buff its power and get to draw cards; you just need to find some ways to enable it.

name: Kobayashi Maru Scenario
prose: The Kobayashi Maru Scenario is a test given to Starfleet cadets that have command ambitions. It’s an unwinnable test designed to have the cadet experience fear in the face of certain death. If you hope not to lose to it, you’ll have to find a way to beat it. There are some ways, like Rules of Acquisition and Kirk, Commanding Officer , but without them, playing this card will cause you to lose far too often.

name: Lieutenant Commander Data
prose: Perhaps the most beloved character in Star Trek: The Next Generation , Lieutenant Commander Data was a highly sophisticated android whose character arc centered around his quest to better understand humanity. This mythic card does quite a lot if you can enable it. Removing three +1/+1 counters from your creatures to draw cards doesn’t sound all that appealing. However, removing charge counters from fully stationed spacecraft that can easily pick them back up again? That sounds a lot more interesting. Data also grows itself with every noncreature spell cast by either player, which makes it a very relevant threat on most boards.

name: Lt. Cmdr. Geordi La Forge
prose: Another popular character from TNG, Lt. Cmdr. Geordi La Forge sadly doesn’t have an inspiring card here. Doubling up your station abilities isn’t all that good. I can’t imagine this will be necessary for any blue decks, so even if you do play it, you won’t miss it when you don’t draw it.

name: Make It So
prose: This is a draw spell I really like. Picard’s catchphrase, Make It So , lets you draw two cards and create a 1/1 token, which sounds pretty good for just 4 mana. It also has you face a dilemma, which makes it very desirable for any decks that care about that. As long as the format is slow enough to allow you to draw cards in this way, this should be a very good card in any blue deck. Bonus points for being part of an infinite combo with Stella Lee, Wild Card .

name: Marooned
prose: The latest sets have had very good variations on this effect in blue, but Marooned is missing the clause of removing the abilities of the thing it enchants. As it stands, it’s a fine way to remove a creature, but it’s not without significant downsides that will surely hold it back compared to cards like Infinite Coursework .

name: Melkotian Adjudicator
prose: Since this triggers off not just instants and sorceries, but also some creatures, I quite like it. It’d be easy to compare it to Cetacean Ops , but the fact that it flies makes a big difference. Flying seems especially rare in Star Trek , since many of the fliers require stationing, which makes Melkotian Adjudicator stand out even more.

name: Mr. Spock, Science Officer
prose: Perhaps the most recognizable character in all of Star Trek , Leonard Nimoy’s Mr. Spock, Science Officer is a unique card that can double every single card you draw . Normally, these effects don’t let you draw an additional card in the draw step, but Spock does. It may not prompt you to draw a card like Quantum Riddler might, but your opponent can’t possibly allow Spock to live for too long since you’ll be drawing two cards every turn. I’m inclined to say Spock is very good. It just needs to survive long enough to give you the value you’re due.

name: Nyota Uhura, Communications
prose: Lieutenant Uhura, played by the wonderful Nichelle Nichols, made waves as one of the first black television characters in a major role in any genre, let alone science fiction. When you play Nyota Uhura, Communications , you should probably name 2 or 3, as they’re the most common mana values of cards in Limited decks. As we get more used to the format, I’m sure a more accurate choice will present itself. If you play Uhura on turn 3, on the play, then choosing 3 will usually net you at least one card, and hopefully more as the game progresses. While it won’t always pan out as you want, I think Uhura will draw you cards enough of the time to warrant a high pick.

name: Open Communications
prose: I love this little card. We’re not typically in the habit of casting 1-mana cantrips without some good reason to do so, but Open Communications will surely act more like a Think Twice . It’s also a great, cheap way to trigger the many cards that care about noncreature spells.

name: Romulan Bird-of-Prey
prose: Two mana for a 4/4 with flying is obviously an excellent deal, but you have to go through a few extra steps to get there with Romulan Bird-of-Prey . You could station it if you wish, but you can also get there just by casting noncreature spells as you normally would. I only wish that your reward for doing so was better than a vanilla flier. I’m sure this card will be fine, but it’s not something I’d look to take highly.

name: Rules of Acquisition
prose: For the most part, Rules of Acquisition looks unplayable to me. Stealing an opponent’s creature is an extremely powerful effect, but allowing your opponent to draw three cards in exchange feels like a trade I never want to make. I think the best way to use this would be to donate something to your opponent and draw three cards, but that’s still not a good exchange unless you give away something truly useless. Overall, it’s just not worth it without some specific use.

name: Scotty, Miracle Worker
prose: His Scottish accent may have been questionable at best, but James Doohan’s Scotty, Miracle Worker became an integral part of sci-fi history as the Enterprise ’s chief engineer. As soon as I heard about the beam me up mechanic, I immediately assumed Scotty’s card would use it, maybe even give it to all the cards in your graveyard. And hey, that’s exactly what Scotty does! You still need to have access to some creatures to bounce to pay for the costs, but getting to recast even one or two good spells will make playing Scotty well worth those costs.

name: Seven of Nine, Unassimilated
prose: Seven of Nine is without a doubt one of the most interesting characters in the whole franchise. Rescued from the Borg by the crew of Voyager , she embarks on a journey to reclaim her humanity and individuality. Seven of Nine, Unassimilated portrays her at the end of her story, as Captain of the new Enterprise-G . This card can’t do much in combat until you have enough lands, but giving you a free loot every turn is good enough in the meantime. I don’t think getting to seven different lands is that unreasonable, and five should be pretty easy in the right deck, which makes Seven quite a reasonable payoff for this archetype.

name: Starfleet Spanner Jockey
prose: On top of being an excellent early blocker, Starfleet Spanner Jockey is quite good at stationing spacecraft. Not being able to attack most of the time might hinder it somewhat, but a 3/3 for 2 mana in Star Trek still has plenty of uses.

name: Subcommander T'Pol
prose: Subcommander T'Pol is quite a powerful creature. I’d already be very happy to have a Frost Lynx with flash , effectively giving you an additional turn of that creature being stunned. The real bonus here is the ability to counter an activated or triggered ability, which Tishana's Tidebinder has shown us can be quite devastating in the right scenarios. The choice of one or the other is incredible too, and it even presents a dilemma, making T’Pol a high pick in Draft.

name: Suurok-Class Science Vessel
prose: It’s 3 mana and it draws a card. I’m sold. While I doubt this will be as good as cantrip creatures of the past, Suurok-Class Science Vessel still has all the hallmarks of a brilliant common for blue. It even has one of the smallest station requirements at just five charge counters, meaning the various engineer cards should have it up and running in no time at all.

name: Suus Mahna Practitioner
prose: “Tapper” creatures tend to appear in white, so this card is throwing me off somewhat. The first two land names are pretty trivial, so Suus Mahna Practitioner should never cost more than 3 mana to activate. I also think the third and fourth should be relatively easy to find, so I’m sure we’ll be Vulcan Nerve Pinching our opponents with relative ease.

name: Test of Priorities
prose: Instant speed flicker spells aren’t printed too often anymore, so it’s nice to see this one here. For the most part, Test of Priorities is a cheap cantrip for both the dilemmas deck and the noncreature spells deck. It might be able to save a creature from removal or reuse its abilities, but you’ll use it most often as a cantrip, and that’s probably good enough to play it.

name: Those Old Scientists
prose: Those Old Scientists is a fine draw spell if you have something to get back with the second chapter, but it loses you card advantage if you don’t. I don’t think a lot of decks will be interested in playing this, but it’s certainly not out of the question in a good noncreature spells build.

name: V'Ger, the Intruder
prose: This is one hell of a big payoff for a ramp deck . V'Ger, the Intruder does everything I want out of a 7-drop. As a 5/7 flier, it should close out games relatively quickly. It immediately draws a card when it enters and then again whenever it attacks, but if you’re worried about getting attacked, it can shrink opposing creatures instead. You can’t just put a 7-drop into your deck, but any deck with a bit of mana acceleration will be happy to pick this up.

name: Vulcan Mind-Meld
prose: The Vulcan Mind-Meld is a skill whereby Vulcans can share their thoughts with other living beings and vice versa. This card is a very cool top-down design of that idea, but essentially letting my opponent draw a card feels like too high a price for me to draw two, especially when they don’t even come from my own library.

name: Wesley Crusher, Starfleet Cadet
prose: “Shut up Wesley!” – Captain Picard Perhaps one of the most divisive characters in Star Trek , Wesley Crusher was a young upstart boy genius who aspired to become a full Starfleet officer. I personally loved the character, but there we go. Wesley Crusher, Starfleet Cadet has a lot of possible options going for it. While each of these options are relatively weak and situational, the fact that you get two of them gives all sorts of possibilities. On top of that, it’s a great candidate to beam up, removes tokens , creates dilemmas, and more. Wesley is a great card even with such narrow abilities.

name: Zefram Cochrane, Warp Pioneer
prose: Played by the brilliant James Cromwell in Star Trek: First Contact , Zefram Cochrane, Warp Pioneer was the inventor of warp drive who made first contact with the Vulcans, ushering in an era of peace for the whole world. Getting to play artifacts from the top of your library is quite a powerful ability, but it’s still possible that you just won’t see anything when you play this pilot . It’s definitely worth playing Cochrane in an artifact-centric deck, but I’m a little apprehensive that it does little else if you don’t get to cast any spells with it.

name: Armus, Skin of Evil
prose: In one of TNG’s most unexpected episodes, the crew discover a planet inhabited by only a single lifeform: Armus, Skin of Evil . They try to engage with it and… let’s just say it goes very wrong for them. This card is really powerful, too. I honestly prefer it as just a good 3-mana removal spell, but coming down on 7-mana and pressuring the opponent’s hand can also be devastating in the right matchup.

name: Assault Drone
prose: +1/+0 to your team certainly isn’t nothing, and the more aggressive you are, the more you’ll appreciate it. But Assault Drone only looks average to me, as not buffing toughness or making your Borg drones more resilient in any way is a shame.

name: Automated Warfare System
prose: This card comes from a very evocative episode of TNG. The crew finds a planet whose population was completely wiped out by automated weaponized drones from a weapons company who just wanted to sell more weapons. Automated Warfare System can cover a few bases as an artifact creature for the Borg and a sacrifice outlet for the Klingons.

name: Bat'leth
prose: Three mana to give -2/-2 is pretty inefficient by most standards, but the classic Klingon Bat'leth gives you quite a bit more than that, leaving behind a very relevant piece of equipment in addition to the removal. We’ve seen this play out twice now in the last couple of sets; Lich's Relic was one of the best cards in Reality Fracture and Crude Bent Blade was among the best commons in The Hobbit . I’m sure this Klingon weapon will be very similar.

name: Battle-Scarred Survivalist
prose: I get that the Klingon deck is going to have a sacrifice theme, but I don’t think Battle-Scarred Survivalist looks that good. We’ve seen Unruly Mob in past sets be virtually unplayable, and this feels like a watered down version of that. Having menace and the right support at least bumps it up a grade, but I’d need to see this Klingon deck in action before I rate it any higher.

name: Blastoneuron
prose: This theme of having cards leave your graveyard for value appears to be well-supported. Blastoneuron ’s enters trigger isn’t the most useful thing you can do, but having a flying creature sit around and trigger over and over sounds pretty good to me. It’s surely not going to trigger as often as something like Falkenrath Noble , but if you can support it properly, it might be closer to that than you’d think.

name: Cha'DIch Investigator
prose: Five-drops tend to be very replaceable these days, yet Cha'DIch Investigator looks surprisingly good for a common, kind of like Girder Goons from Streets of New Capenna . A 4/4 plus a 2/1 haste creature is worth paying 5 mana for, and I can see this being good top-end for the mana curve of your Klingon aggro decks.

name: Collation Trimatrix
prose: The main reason Cryptbreaker was so good back in the day was for this ability right here. Collation Trimatrix may not be able to create any tokens , but getting to draw a card just by tapping three of your Borg is an incredible ability. If you’re lucky enough to curve this on turn 1 into Assembly Specialist on 2, I doubt you’ll lose that game. This is an awesome payoff for the Borg, something I’d be happy to take early and build around.

name: Collective Drone
prose: The problem with a 10/2 creature is that as ridiculous as that stat line might seem at first, it still just trades off with other 2-drops in combat. Collective Drone won’t always be that big, but the simple fact that it never gains any toughness makes it fragile. If you can give it some other abilities through your other Borg drones, then it certainly pays you off for that. But until then, it’s little more than a slightly over-statted vanilla creature .

name: Commander Raffi Musiker
prose: Most of the time, you’re going to want to investigate with Commander Raffi Musiker . A 3-drop Thraben Inspector is pretty strong, even at the cost of 2 life. Exiling something from a graveyard doesn’t seem like it will be as good, but if you have some gravebreak triggered abilities available, I could also see that working. Overall, Raffi covers a lot of bases and slots perfectly into multiple decks as a result.

name: D'Ghor Bloodletter
prose: Given how common the 2/1 Klingon tokens and the 1/1 Officer tokens are, the ability to give -1/-1 to all creatures sounds like it could be quite devastating. D'Ghor Bloodletter , despite being a Klingon, is actually a great weapon for fighting against the Klingon decks, and the Fleshbag Marauder mode is a nice buyout for the right situation, too.

name: Death Is Irrelevant
prose: Weirdly enough, Death Is Irrelevant looks basically unplayable in Borg decks. Casting an 8-mana spell in a low-curve aggressive deck simply isn’t going to happen. That said, if you have a deck that can resolve an 8-mana spell, then this will almost always win you the game. Reanimating an indestructible creature from either graveyard every single turn, including the one where you play this, gets out of hand extremely quickly. What’s especially nice about this is how likely we are to have big creatures in graveyards thanks to the landcyclers, so there should always be something for you to bring back.

name: The Destruction of Praxis
prose: Board wipes are very powerful in Limited, but the biggest downside they have is that your opponent gets the initiative to make the first play after the dust settles. If you have six different lands in play, sweeping away all creatures and then creating a pair of 2/1s with haste is an absurd effect. I’m still unsure as to how easy it’ll be to get up to six different lands, but assuming it’s regularly possible, The Destruction of Praxis has a chance at being among the best cards in Star Trek .

name: De-evolve
prose: This is certainly an interesting way to word a Pacifism in black. For the most part, this will function the same way, but later in the game you’ll get to exile the creature as soon as the turn starts, which is pretty nice. However, De-evolve comes with no protection against the enchanted creature being beamed up, so you have to be very careful to choose your moment. As such, it’s a good removal spell, but there are much better ones.

name: Eject the Warp Core
prose: Vayne's Treachery was among the best commons in Final Fantasy Limited with good reason. The ability to kill any big creature for just 2 mana, even at the cost of another sacrifice, is very powerful. Eject the Warp Core is exactly the same card, and I have no trouble assuming it’ll be just as good in this setting.

name: Elim Garak, Simple Tailor
prose: There are so many dilemmas you can face in this set that I’m definitely keeping my eye on any and all dilemma payoffs. Elim Garak, Simple Tailor looks like a very strong one to me. It may not give you card advantage, but a 4-point total life swing can be obscenely powerful, and it doesn’t even come with a once per turn clause. Given that we’ve seen many dilemmas that cost very little mana, I could see Garak trigger several times in a turn and really put a lot of pressure on your opponent.

name: Fugitive Listener
prose: The typical Ravenous Rats design has been losing a bit of luster lately, so changing it up and putting that same ability on a 3-drop with a bit more power sounds alright to me. Fugitive Listener won’t draw you a card, but having your opponent discard one is nearly always just as good, which makes this a premium black common.

name: Gabriel Lorca, Mirror Menace
prose: The surprising villain of Star Trek: Discovery ’s first season, played by the brilliant Jason Isaacs, Gabriel Lorca, Mirror Menace is a pretty annoying card. A 5/4 with menace for 5 mana isn’t all that great, but the ability to keep bringing Lorca back whenever you face a dilemma certainly paints it in a new light. It’s both a dilemma payoff, and a card that keeps leaving your graveyard. I think you need to find the right deck for it, but Lorca will be pretty powerful if you find it.

name: General Chang, Cold Warrior
prose: What usually holds sacrifice decks back is their lack of good, cheap sacrifice outlets. General Chang, Cold Warrior is very cheap both to cast and to activate, but it also gives you an extremely powerful effect, putting counters on all of your Klingons at once. This is a great payoff for that deck, as well as being a useful 1-drop to start off your curve as early as possible.

name: Georgiou, Terran Emperor
prose: Georgiou, Terran Emperor is a fun and unique design for a 6-drop. As much as I’d love to go down to 0 life and start creating hordes of officer tokens, the fact that you’ll lose as soon as it leaves play makes this strategy a bit delicate. Though if your opponent can’t remove it at all, you’ll inevitably win. Georgiou is going to be a temperamental card for sure, but one I’m definitely willing to try out.

name: A Good Day to Die
prose: Even just for 1 mana, A Good Day to Die isn’t a combat trick I’m ever happy to play. We’ve seen some defensible versions of this effect in the past, but they all do much better than simply drawing you a card, like leaving a token behind or reanimating the creature. This new version just doesn’t cut it for me.

name: Grand Nagus Zek
prose: The Ferengi, introduced in Star Trek: The Next Generation , are basically extremist capitalists, where their entire culture and society is built around the acquisition of wealth no matter the cost. So, of course Grand Nagus Zek and the other Ferengi we see here will be Treasure -themed. Creating a free Treasure whenever something dies is pretty good on its own, especially in a Klingon deck where we expect our creatures to die more often. I don’t know what I make of Zek then getting bigger, because the Treasures are probably best used as further sacrifice fodder or mana acceleration. Either way, just playing it as a 3-mana Pitiless Plunderer should be good enough.

name: Gul Dukat, Colonial Prefect
prose: The villainous Cardassian, Gul Dukat, Colonial Prefect , probably won’t do as much damage in Magic as the character did in Star Trek . While the card’s ability is certainly interesting, the fact it costs 7 mana is a significant drawback. While 7-drops are definitely castable in modern Limited formats, they need to make a much bigger impact to the board than this, especially as Gul Dukat might not even do anything on the turn you play it. I think my grade is quite generous here. It might just be unplayable with the way the format shapes up.

name: He's Dead, Jim
prose: Well, every set worth its salt has one of these. Four mana to destroy any creature at instant speed and give a minor bonus on top is always good, usually one of the best commons in the set, and nothing else needs to be said about it. I do love the theming of using one of McCoy’s best-known lines, He's Dead, Jim , as the card’s name.

name: Hive Mind Coprocessor
prose: If you have successfully “gone wide” by the time you play this card, you should theoretically be able to get an attack in and probably draw several cards for doing so. The fact that you don’t need to pay mana into the triggers from Hive Mind Coprocessor makes it a lot easier to use, too. I can definitely see this being the top-end you need for a good Borg deck, especially as the extra cards should help you to keep applying pressure in future turns.

name: Impossible Choice
prose: The season two episode of Voyager , “Tuvix”, posited one of the show’s best and most well-known ethical conundrums.
