Tuvok and Neelix end up fused together into one person, and the entire episode is spent debating whether it’s ethical to split them back into their original selves. I don’t know the answer, but I do know that you should probably pick “remain fused” whenever you play this card, though neither modes of this Impossible Choice look like great options to me.

name: In the Pale Moonlight
prose: One of Deep Space Nine ’s best episodes, In the Pale Moonlight sees Captain Sisko reflecting on the personal cost he’s paid in attempting to trick the Romulan empire into joining the Federation’s war against the Dominion. This saga tells that story pretty well and is a very strong card to play. It reminds me of The Eldest Reborn , where every chapter of the saga gives you another bit of value, and I’m all here for that.

name: Kai Winn, Faithless Leader
prose: To make the most of Kai Winn, Faithless Leader , you’d want some kind of prior knowledge of your opponent’s hand and/or deck. This card gets a lot better in an open decklists environment, but going in blind? It’ll more often than not be a 3/1 for 2 with very little upside. At the very least you can name a common removal spell in your opponent’s colors, but you’ll get it wrong most of the time.

name: Khan, Vengeful Heart
prose: Khan Noonien Singh is perhaps Star Trek ’s most legendary villain. The mythic representing him is quite strong in Limited, but casting Khan from exile isn’t likely to happen too often. Not a lot of things in Star Trek will exile it, but just casting Khan, Vengeful Heart once to sacrifice something and draw two cards is good enough.

name: Obsidian Order Operative
prose: Facing dilemmas in TRK seems fairly trivial to do. I like having access to a trigger that drains my opponent with each dilemma I face, and a 2/5 makes for a fairly resilient blocker, but Obsidian Order Operative isn’t exciting me like it should. It’s a bit dull, and very cuttable, but it does at least do something that I might want in my dilemma decks.

name: Organic Avulsion Unit
prose: Menace on one creature isn’t a problem. Your opponent can usually deal with it without too much fuss. But menace on your whole team? That’s dangerous. Consider a board where both players have three creatures. If you give all your creatures menace and attack, your opponent can only block one of them, leaving them to get hit by the other two! For this simple reason, Organic Avulsion Unit actually looks pretty scary, despite its weak stats.

name: Overflow Submatrix
prose: I don’t think I had a new riff on Lurrus of the Dream-Den on my bingo card for Star Trek , but it does look like that’s what we have in Overflow Submatrix . They may come with finality counters , but the ability to recast any artifact creature in your graveyard over the next few turns is incredible. I’d always try to wait for an opening where I can cast this with, say, 5 mana available, allowing me to get a free 2-drop on the same turn I play it, then hope it survives long enough to get more free creatures. This card is incredible, and a great early sign to draft a Borg deck.

name: Pattern Buffer Preservation
prose: This card reminds me a lot of Final Fantasy ’s Resentful Revelation . While Pattern Buffer Preservation doesn’t give you as much card selection, the vastly cheaper beam me up cost means you’ll get to cast both copies of it a lot more often. It’ll almost always be a two-for-one card advantage spell, and I’m sure there are plenty of decks that will want that.

name: Relentless Drednok
prose: It may not have evasion , but getting to play a Relentless Drednok on turn 1, especially in a Borg deck, is a great way to start off your mana curve. Lifelink is very powerful, even on small creatures, and getting to turn it into a free card later in the game makes it a great card to sacrifice, too. It basically does something in nearly every one of black’s themes and that’s worth the grade on its own.

name: Resistance Is Futile
prose: We don’t see a lot of clean 2-mana removal spells anymore. While Star Trek does have a considerable number of artifact creatures, including all of the spacecraft, Resistance Is Futile still answers a lot of creatures that need to be dealt with. Unlike Go for the Throat , it has a very reasonable extra mode that you can use instead. This is an incredible removal spell, and it’s ticking a lot of boxes for this format.

name: Rogue Artificial Intelligence
prose: Just like the other landcyclers, the fact that this is mana fixing is the main reason to play it. When you do play it on 6, Rogue Artificial Intelligence will have a significant impact on the board no matter which mode you choose, while also being an artifact creature for the Borg and a dilemma for blue/black. This might actually be the best entry in the cycle.

name: Salt Vampire
prose: We really have come a long way since the days of Mesmeric Fiend . We don’t see new versions of this effect very often, but when we do, it’s often an upgrade on the previous one. Salt Vampire is an excellent play on turn 2. Even if it’s going to die at some point, taking a card out of your opponent’s hand for a while will mess up the plays they were planning to make. You should probably always take a cheap removal spell that could kill this, but no matter what you take, this should be pretty effective.

name: Sela, Tal Shiar Paradox
prose: One of the most memorable plot twists in TNG was the reveal of this Romulan character, played by Denise Crosby, whose own main character on the show, Tasha Yar, had been killed off a few seasons prior. Sela, Tal Shiar Paradox is first and foremost an excellent payoff for the black/green graveyard deck. While it’s a self-contained advantage engine, getting to attack with Sela doesn’t seem too promising when it’s only a 3/3 for 4 mana. Even without attacking, sitting back and generating free tokens whenever something leaves your graveyard is an excellent way to spend your mana, so long as you surround it with the right support.

name: Storied Veteran
prose: This aggressive Klingon card does a few things on its own. Firstly, the fact that it can come back makes it an excellent creature to sacrifice. Bringing it back of course causes it to leave the graveyard, so it’s also good in black/green. Being an aggressive creature might make it reasonably playable in the Borg deck too, even though it isn’t an artifact. Storied Veteran looks like a pretty solid little 1-drop to me.

name: Stray from History
prose: I’m never a big fan of Coercion effects, but Soul Salvage is definitely something I can get behind. Stray from History looks like a very solid common that I’ll probably always want at least one copy of in a black deck.

name: Tal Shiar Operative
prose: This creature essentially attacks as a 2/2 with deathtouch , which is going to be pretty hard for a lot of opponents to block profitably. As such, Tal Shiar Operative is a simple enough common that can provide you with a repeatable source of dilemmas. That’s definitely useful to some decks.

name: Tell Me What You See
prose: In this classic TNG episode, Picard is captured by the Romulans and is subjected to psychological torture through gaslighting. His captor keeps insisting that he’s being shown five lights when there are only four, but our intrepid Captain never compromises, always repeating that there are just four lights. While Tell Me What You See uses a punisher mechanic that we don’t often like, the fact that it’s repeatable as long as you keep facing dilemmas makes it look very appealing. I think this is going to be a really cool build-around for this deck and I’m excited to see where it lands.

name: Tenacious Drone
prose: While I’d prefer the stats of this creature to be the other way around (a 1/1 that dies into a 2/1), Tenacious Drone is still a high quality 2-drop that doesn’t mind being sacrificed. It clearly should work in the Borg deck, but it’s probably good enough for the Klingon sacrifice deck, too.

name: Test of Loyalty
prose: Given the black/green theme, I can definitely see wanting there to be a Raise Dead in this format, and here it is. You’ll use Test of Loyalty most often simply to get a creature back, as guaranteeing yourself a castable spell is pretty much always better than drawing a random card. It’s also a cheap spell for noncreature spell synergies and a dilemma for you to face. This is an excellent card that I think a lot of black decks will be after.

name: U.S.S. Reliant, From Hell's Heart
prose: The Reliant is the ship in Wrath of Khan that Khan commandeers and takes into battle against Kirk and the Enterprise . U.S.S. Reliant, From Hell's Heart looks like it has a lot of potential. Reanimating one creature right away makes it worth spending the mana to play it, even though 10 charge counters is a lot to accrue if you want to attack with it. Once you do reach 10 counters, reanimating a creature whenever this hits an opponent is a huge bonus, and not one that your opponent can ever let you get to.

name: Vengeance Mission
prose: Building this up to seven quest counters sounds like quite a lot. It’s worth noting that creatures trading off in combat will of course trigger this twice, so maybe seven counters isn’t too difficult, but I’d still view Vengeance Mission as only hitting your opponent for 1 each time it triggers. That’s probably still good enough to play, but we’ve seen significantly better versions of this same effect in the past, so I think its power level is a bit below where it needs to be.

name: Academy Instructor
prose: Like most playable Young Pyromancer variants, Academy Instructor is still cheap enough to be worth playing. On top of that, it also triggers with every noncreature spell you cast, not just instants and sorceries. This is the perfect build-around for the red/blue archetype, and it also puts a lot of extra power onto the board for red/white.

name: Beckett Mariner, Impetuous Ensign
prose: I’m sure I’m missing something having not watched Lower Decks , but Beckett Mariner, Impetuous Ensign ’s card design leaves a little to be desired. It’s basically just a 2/1 with first strike, which is of course a good creature, but it has a lot of extra text that really doesn’t amount to much. Mariner hits your opponent for an extra 2 damage every three times you tap it. That’s it. It’s good enough to play, but it’s not exciting at all.

name: Boarding Action
prose: Getting to play Boarding Action on turn 2 and immediately attack is a great way to start a curve. Later in the game, you might even find a good spot to cast this twice with its beam me up cost and get a great attack in with your two new haste creatures . This looks like an excellent red common that most of red’s archetypes will be very happy to play.

name: Brazen Bluff
prose: I absolutely love the design of this card. Big bluffs like this were a quintessential part of Captain Kirk’s character and style of command. Sadly, the most common outcome of Brazen Bluff is basically a Negate , so it’s not at all playable in Limited. I’m looking forward to playing it in Standard , though.

name: Cantankerous Captain
prose: Cantankerous Captain brings back the design we saw on Valor Singer from Forgotten Realms and adds a pretty mediocre bonus once you have 8 power among your creatures. You’re going to be able to find much better creatures for your aggro decks, but this will fill the curve in fine.

name: Captain James T. Kirk
prose: Few characters in science fiction are quite as prolific as William Shatner’s Captain James T. Kirk . As Captain of the Enterprise , he never shied away from getting his hands dirty, and hand-to-hand brawls were common in the original series. As the character didn’t believe in no-win scenarios, it stands to reason that this card’s ability would get stronger when you have no options left in your hand. While none of Kirk’s modes are all that strong, having it trigger on entering and attacking means they’ll add up very quickly. This is an incredible design for an iconic character, and one of the cards in TRK I’m most looking forward to trying.

name: Captain Michael Burnham
prose: The adoptive sister of Spock, Captain Michael Burnham of the U.S.S. Discovery is a somewhat contentious figure in the Star Trek universe, but a capable Captain nonetheless. As for the card, this is a pretty solid payoff for this red/green landfall deck. The points of damage aren’t all that important, but there appears to be a lot of ways to get multiple land drops in a turn and have Michael pick up +1/+1 counters, too. Given that it starts out as a 3/3 with trample, it looks like Burnham will become a threat very quickly.

name: Captain's Tutelage
prose: We’ve seen plenty of cards similar to Captain's Tutelage in the past, and they’ve never really panned out. An effect like this isn’t exactly guaranteed to win a combat for you, and you certainly won’t win the next after it has resolved. Whether or not I bump this grade up or even further down depends completely on how well-placed combat tricks end up being in the format.

name: D-7 Battle Cruiser
prose: Creating a temporary 2/1 token with haste every turn isn’t a bad effect in theory, but is it worth the cost for this card? I’m not entirely sure. These tokens can be pretty useful in the early game, and they give you a free sacrifice every turn, but once they’re outclassed in combat, they’re very difficult to get any advantage from. This D-7 Battle Cruiser looks to be on the weak side for a rare spacecraft, but I could be wrong.

name: Dahar Master
prose: Finding the sacrifice fodder for Dahar Master is the only thing you need to do here. If you sacrifice a creature with 2 power, a Shock in exchange isn’t actually a good trade for you. It’s not that this card is bad, but you need to make sure that what you give up is worth what you get out of it. If you don’t have much to offer to it, this can probably stay in the sideboard.

name: Dominion Infiltration
prose: Creating temporary clones like this isn’t a winning play, especially when you need to target your opponent’s creatures with it. You have no control over how good Dominion Infiltration will be when you maindeck it, which is a surefire recipe for a terrible, unplayable card.

name: Encounter the Unknown
prose: Two damage to all creatures is the base rate on this card, and I think that should be pretty good. We’ve seen a lot of small creatures in the format so far, which leads me to believe it’ll be quite effective. Also, the fact that you can trade Encounter the Unknown for two cards from your deck if you don’t need it is a really nice buyout when you come against creatures too big for you to destroy.

name: Erica Ortegas, Plucky Pilot
prose: Landfall decks often have difficulty with running out of lands to keep triggering their effects, so Erica Ortegas, Plucky Pilot sounds like a reasonable effect to have access to, since it makes it so that you can keep playing lands every turn. The problem is, as a 3/3 haste creature for 4 mana, it’s a bit too weak to stand on its own. Overall, Ortegas is a weak synergy piece that won’t even be necessary in every landfall deck.

name: Exploratory Mission
prose: This is a very interesting card advantage engine. It essentially reads as Landfall: Draw a spell”, which honestly sounds really powerful. Like the other cards in this cycle, Exploratory Misson is a 4-mana enchantment that doesn’t affect the board, so its power level is naturally limited.

name: Genesis Effect
prose: In Wrath of Khan , the Genesis Effect is the process by which a dead planetoid can be transformed into a planet full of life, but it also destroys any trace of life in its path. As such, the effect of this card is a wonderful top-down design. Six damage for 5 mana is also efficient enough that most red decks should be happy to play the first copy.

name: Horta
prose: Poor old Colossal Dreadmaw , another victim of power creep in the 2020s. Horta is a strong creature if you cast it, but the main reason to put it in your deck is because of its landcycling, just like the other entries in this cycle.

name: Infinite Diversity
prose: As noble a cause as Infinite Diversity is, it’s a 9-mana spell. It’s pretty close to uncastable in most situations, and it requires a good spell to copy and plenty of creatures in play to fuel it, all of which add up to an unplayable mythic .

name: Khaaaaaaaaaaaannn!
prose: This heavily memed moment from Wrath of Khan obviously had to be made into a card of its own, but I don’t have to like it. The card is a fine piece of removal. Khaaaaaaaaaaaannn! will deal 2 damage for 2 mana, 4 damage for 3, 6 damage for 4, and so on. These are all good rates, and the combination of all of them in the same card is really good.

name: Khan, Despot by Design
prose: I’m very high on Khan, Despot by Design given the context of set. We’ve seen a lot of creatures with only 1 toughness, including the 1/1 Officer and 2/1 Klingon tokens. That should mean that Khan has a lot of opportunities to come down and devastate a board. On top of that, it’s also a big trample creature that’s kind of hard to deal with in its own right.

name: La'An Noonien-Singh, Security
prose: Since La'An Noonien-Singh, Security only requires you to attack to trigger, you can often trigger it on the same turn you play it. With at least 4 power already on the board, La’an can come down and allow you to attack profitably past a single blocker. From there, the ability to take a blocker out of the equation each turn should allow you to attack far more often, making this a pretty strong card for an aggressive red deck.

name: Lwaxana Troi, Charming Guest
prose: Lwaxana Troi has Deanna’s mother who could read people’s minds thanks to her Betazoid heritage. As such, she’d often exclaim that Picard or other men around her are thinking about her in a sexual way to embarrass and flirt with them. As such, is it not a bit on the nose that her card, Lwaxana Troi, Charming Guest , can give a bonus to a creature you have as long as this card is… horizontal? Yeah, okay. I think it’s good, don’t get me wrong, just the design is a bit… funny?

name: Munitions Enthusiast
prose: You don’t need any additional abilities to make a 3/2 trample for 2 mana worth playing. Munitions Enthusiast is a great early play in any red deck, and it trades up extremely well, since the 1 extra point of damage will help it kill bigger creatures in combat.

name: The Naked Time
prose: The Naked Time was the fourth episode of the original series of Star Trek . In this episode, an infection spreads throughout the crew leaving them feeling intoxicated, leading to all sorts of weird incidents. This card, unfortunately, doesn’t look very good. It does a few things, but none of them are worth spending a whole card to get them. Maybe a dedicated landfall deck can make sure of the extra mountain on chapter one.

name: Pah-Wraith
prose: Most decks you build will have at least two differently named lands. Namely, the two basic lands for your two colors. As such, Pah-Wraith will basically always attack as a 6/4 with first strike at minimum. On top of that, giving +2/+0 to your team looks pretty good. The problem is that this is a 7-drop that’s best suited for a low-curve aggro deck, which doesn’t want 7-drops. It looks good, but I have a feeling it’s just too expensive to be the massive bomb that I think it could be.

name: Perils of the Past
prose: First thing’s first, using this as a combat trick is a bad idea. It should probably be what you do around 5% of the time. About a quarter of the cards in this set are artifacts, which is just enough to make artifact removal look like something you want to put in your main deck. Between the Borg and the spacecraft, there are a lot of good targets. I’d definitely start out by playing the first copy of Perils of the Past in my main deck, and as the format evolves we can adjust that number accordingly.

name: Planetary Bombardment
prose: One mana for 4 damage is truly an absurd rate, which is why Flame Slash still sees play in Vintage Cubes to this day. Planetary Bombardment is mostly just a sorcery speed Shock , but the fact that it does have this potential to kill bigger creatures so cheaply is likely to make it one of the best red commons, if not the best overall.

name: Planetary Patrol
prose: Assuming you hit your land drops, at least for the first few turns of the game, Planetary Patrol will basically be a 3/3 for 2 mana whenever it attacks. That’s pretty good, and the base of a 2/2 for 2 is perfectly fine. I don’t know if I necessarily want it outside of a landfall deck, but it does look solid.

name: Plasma Cascade
prose: Plasma Cascade isn’t exactly Lightning Strike , but it’s still a good deal for 3 mana. I love the extra bonus that’s been tacked onto it too, as trading an excess land for a better card is very close to just drawing a card.

name: Q, Stacking the Deck
prose: John De Lancie’s mysterious “Q” was a recurring villain from The Next Generation who also showed up in Deep Space Nine and Voyager , a seemingly omnipotent being who would act as a constant annoyance to Picard and the rest of the Enterprise crew. And this weird card design really does suit him. Sometimes, you’ll play Q, Stacking the Deck , exile a pretty weak spell and not much will happen. But, if you exile anything good with it, then every single card you draw, lands included, can become copies of that card. If you hit a bomb rare, a removal spell, or anything else on that level, you basically win the game. Even though its ability has an element of randomness, it’s still a 4/4 on the board, doesn’t need to survive for its ability to remain active, and has the potential to completely take over the game. What an awesome card!

name: Quark, Humble Proprietor
prose: I really don’t know what to make of Deep Space Nine ’s humble Ferengi barkeep, Quark, Humble Proprietor . It’s a really unique design that basically requires you to sacrifice it at some point to accomplish anything at all. But even when you do, your only reward is a bunch of Treasure tokens. I can see Quark being a great card in a dedicated sacrifice deck, where the Treasures act as perfect sacrifice fodder, but in your average red deck, I think it falls well short of the mark.

name: Ravenous Cosmozoan
prose: While the dream is to cast this for just 1 mana, even at 3 or 4, Ravenous Cosmozoan looks like a great card to cast. Flying appears to be at a premium in this set, so a 3/3 flier will go a long way. It won’t take much to set this up to be playable and a really good spells deck might get to utilize it even more.

name: Reckless Impulse
prose: Unlike most draw spells, Reckless Impulse isn’t great to play early in a game. It is, however, a very nice card to draw later in the game, as you’re far more likely to have enough time and mana to play both cards you hit with it. All I’ll say otherwise is to remember not to play your land for turn before playing this, because if you hit two lands with it, you’ll really want to be able to play both over two turns.

name: Red Alert!
prose: Okay, Red Dwarf is the first thing I think of when I hear “Red Alert!”, not Star Trek , but so be it. This card is crap anyway. Trumpet Blast is basically never playable and getting a cost reduction on the worst turn to play it isn’t even an upside.

name: Sarcophagus, Ship of the Dead
prose: A lot of the value of Sarcophagus, Ship of the Dead is given to you up front, as even before it’s stationed, it’s basically an Orcish Oriflamme . Of course that’s not enough to justify the whole grade; that +1/+0 boost not only helps you in combat, but also helps you to station. Ten charge counters is a lot, but between its own trigger and power boosts, that number starts to look a lot smaller, and a 4/4 flier looks incredible in this format.

name: Savvy Profiteer
prose: Savvy Profiteer is mostly just a 2-drop mana dork in red , which is solid on its own. If you have the time, creating Treasure tokens will allow you to build up your mana over a few turns to cast something really big, or it could just give you some stuff to sacrifice. Still, it’s a mana dork, so you’ll play this in every red deck.

name: Silicate Surveyor
prose: Just about any creature that “draws” a card when it enters is worth playing. Silicate Surveyor really pushes that idea to its limit, since a 4/4 reach creature for 5 mana is very far away from something I’d be happy to play otherwise. It’s a fine card, but when it gets this expensive I wonder if we can do better.

name: Starfleet Security
prose: The death trigger is limited to only your turn, but Starfleet Security looks an awful lot like a creature that draws a card when it dies. I don’t make much of it being a 1/1 with haste, but it’s clearly a useful 1-drop that will shine alongside some ways to sacrifice it.

name: Tal Shiar Analyst
prose: Thermo-Alchemist was one of my favorite spells build-arounds from the past. Tal Shiar Analyst , despite costing an additional mana, is practically the same card. That mana definitely matters, but what you get for it is a creature that’s also capable of attacking for more damage and maybe even trading for something in combat if you need it to. For a common, this looks like an immensely powerful card in blue/red.

name: Targ Wrangler
prose: Unlike the Pet Sehlat , Targ Wrangler looks extremely good for an oversized 3-drop with a downside. The thing is, we’ve seen a lot of cards act as sacrifice fodder so far, which means it shouldn’t be too hard to negate this drawback completely. As such, this looks a lot like a big 5/3 that’ll trade off with two creatures in combat. It even works really well with stationing spacecraft and the 8-power theme in red/white.

name: Tasha Yar, Out of Time
prose: Tasha Yar, Out of Time is a fast, aggressive creature with a great death trigger, and you can bring it back later for one final hit. Tasha gives you quite a lot of advantage for a single card; you just have to find ways to make the most of it.

name: Test of Identity
prose: Some decks are going to be perfectly happy casting this as Thrill of Possibility , while Klingon decks are going to want it as a cool combat trick that you can essentially cycle. Test of Identity looks like it hits enough notes that it’ll see play, but it’s not something you should go out of your way to pick up.

name: Transporter Malfunction
prose: I always try to pay attention whenever I see a removal spell that I can cast twice. There are so few removal spells with flashback in the game, let alone ones that are this efficient. You’d happily play Transporter Malfunction even if it didn’t have beam me up, so the fact that it does is a huge boon. This is bound to be one of the best removal spells in Star Trek , and it can even finish off a player.

name: Will Riker, First in the Field
prose: As a frequent member of landing parties, Will Riker, First in the Field is all about landfall. While having no landfall triggers itself, Riker creates two landfall triggers every turn. I naturally worry about running out of lands at some point, but that might be to your benefit, as it means you just draw spells for the rest of the game. I wouldn’t want to run Riker without a good foundation of landfall triggers to make use of it, but it looks really good if you can give it that support.

name: Worf, Intelligence Contractor
prose: Worf was the first Klingon officer to serve in Starfleet, and he’s the most used character in the entire franchise. This card, Worf, Intelligence Contractor leaves quite a bit to be desired. It naturally works very well in a Klingon deck, where you should be able to sacrifice the creature that you steal, but being limited to only stealing smaller creatures will likely hold Worf back.

name: The Wrath of Khan
prose: I’ve mentioned it a few times already, but 1982’s Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan is believed by many Trekkies to be the best Star Trek project ever produced. This card does a reasonable job of telling this story, and it’s quite powerful, too. It’s basically a 3-mana removal spell that deals 4 damage and then has some minor upsides on top, which is something you’d always play.

name: Adversary by Algorithm
prose: Adversary by Algorithm gives us effectively a reprint of Call of the Herd , except with beam me up. I really like that, and with how good Bestial Incursion was in Reality Fracture , I have no problem thinking this will be very good here, too.

name: Amok Time
prose: Known to Trekkies as simply “the one where Spock gets horny”, Amok Time is a classic episode where Spock experiences “Pon Farr”. This requires him to return to Vulcan and meet his arranged mate, but it results in him and Kirk having a fight to the death. This card is a fantastic retelling of that story, and if you play it right, it’ll end up being a removal spell that gets a creature back from your graveyard and even gains you 3 life for good measure. This is an excellent card, and you should take it highly.

name: Astute Terraformer
prose: Rootwalla and similar creatures get to use threat of activation to attack past bigger creatures in the early turns of a game. Astute Terraformer doesn’t, as its ability is still too expensive to activate that early in most games. This isn’t the kind of benefit you need or even want in a Strange New Worlds deck, though 2/2 with upside is still a solid baseline.

name: Branching Timeline
prose: Eight-mana spells need to have some guarantee of winning the game for you to want to bother accelerating into them. Branching Timeline does nothing of the sort and is entirely random, which makes it completely unplayable.

name: Captain Jonathan Archer
prose: I never watched Star Trek: Enterprise , but if I had known that Captain Jonathan Archer had a lovely dog , I might have given it a try sooner. Three mana for a 3/3 plus a 1/1 is a great start, but you also have three creature types between Archer and Porthos, meaning its activated ability will already give +3/+3 at minimum. This will probably let Porthos attack as a 4/4 or bigger, or be able to send some other creatures into combat instead. This is a great card for any green deck just on rate alone.

name: Captain Kathryn Janeway
prose: Captain Kathryn Janeway looks quite strong. Exploring is a fairly random mechanic; you’re not sure what you’re going to get out of it, but allowing every creature you play to explore should help you to smooth out your draws and make sure you’re finding the best spells you can.

name: Captain Pike, Fullness of Time
prose: Most people know who James T. Kirk is, but far fewer will know that in Star Trek ’s pilot episode in 1966, Christopher Pike was in fact the captain of the Enterprise . He was then replaced by William Shatner in the second episode, but since those days, Pike’s character has been explored in the Kelvin timeline films and two of most recent projects: Discovery and Strange New Worlds . Captain Pike, Fullness of Time of course had to use this mechanic and does so quite well. I don’t know how big it’s likely to get, but even if Pike were just a 2/2 that let you play lands off the top of your deck , that would be an excellent card.

name: Cold-Blooded Crew
prose: Our final landcycler, Cold-Blooded Crew looks a fair bit worse than its counterparts in other colors, but that’s neither here nor there. You’ll definitely play it as a way to fix your mana, and if you end up casting it as a 6-drop that can’t be chump blocked, there are far worse things you could do.

name: Common Goal
prose: We do prefer these spells to be instants, but letting two of your creatures team up to destroy another means that Common Goal ought be a very effective removal spell in any green deck. It’ll basically always find something to kill.

name: Culber and Stamets, Star-Crossed
prose: As I watched Discovery , I felt entranced by the beautiful love story between Hugh Culber and Paul Stamets. They go through so many hardships and yet always manage to find each other again, and it was wonderful to watch. Sadly, Culber and Stamets, Star-Crossed doesn’t look like a very good card. A 3/4 plus a +1/+1 counter is fine for 4 mana, but the additional mana mode is baffling to say the least. I think you’ll generally be able to do better than this one.

name: Dathon and Picard at El-Adrel
prose: TNG’s season five episode “Darmok” is probably my favorite in the entire franchise. In it, the Enterprise encounters the Tamarians, a race whose language is seemingly impossible for them to decipher. It turns out that the Tamarians are storytellers and they speak entirely in metaphors and story references, kind of like how many people today communicate through memes. “Temba, His Arms Wide” means to give something and “Shaka, When the Walls Fell” means to fail. It’s a wonderful episode that really highlights Patrick Stewart’s raw acting talent. Anyway, Dathon and Picard at El-Adrel is a pretty crap card, but it’s a wonderful representation of that episode.

name: David and Carol Marcus, Creators
prose: We’ve seen plenty of similar 3-drops that accelerate you with an extra land and they’ve always been great, but David and Carol Marcus, Creators even fixes you for every color by giving you a New Planet token. The card’s just great, and you should play it in every green deck you can.

name: Dominion Assault Force
prose: A 4/4 vigilance creature for 4 isn’t exactly terrible, though I do wish it did a little more than that. A free surveil is definitely nice to have, but not something that elevates Dominion Assault Force beyond being a simple vanilla creature.

name: Dominion Supervisor
prose: It’s quite funny to see a big, scary Dominion agent being barely better than the adorable Pridemalkin . Dominion Supervisor is a nice card to curve into naturally, and it might be quite good in the late game when you have multiple creatures to gain trample , but it’s kind of average overall.

name: Dr. Joseph M'Benga
prose: Dr. Joseph M'Benga is interesting, but the main thing to note about this doctor is that it doesn’t do anything by itself. Doubling all your counters is a good ability to have access to, but unless you’re using counters quite frequently, M’Benga basically does nothing.

name: Dr. Leonard "Bones" McCoy
prose: The final member of our original bridge crew in this review, Dr. Leonard “Bones” McCoy was a brilliant doctor with a good dash of southern charm. His metaphors, hostile personality, and close personal relationship with Captain Kirk turned him into a much-loved character across the whole show. This card is also excellent, basically functioning as a sort of Eternal Witness with flash who can also save a creature from dying if you flash it in at the right time. I’d always play Bones in a green deck, because it’s hard not to get any value from it.

name: Final Frontier
prose: I’m very much not a fan of 3-mana Rampant Growth s, but with the strange new worlds and landfall mechanics, plus the fact that this can fetch a planet dual land , I reckon Final Frontier will be one of the better versions of this effect that we’ve ever seen.

name: First Contact
prose: The black/green archetype in Star Trek is all about cards leaving your graveyard, and we’ve seen several payoffs that reward you for that. Funnily enough, not only does First Contact fill your graveyard for this strategy, but the card you get back also comes from your graveyard, so it’ll trigger all of these effects. I doubt I’d want to play this in any other deck, but it does look very nice in black/green.

name: Genesis Device
prose: As a big fan of Scapeshift in Modern, I’m really liking Genesis Device . The machine capable of turning a lifeless planet into a lush paradise, teeming with life, of course can turn all your lands into new ones. I think the main use of this is simply to ramp you like Final Frontier can. However, in a landfall deck specifically, cracking this to get five or six new landfall triggers sounds promising.

name: Holo-Engineer
prose: Before we even get to the rest of the card, Holo-Engineer starts out life as a 3/3 that creates another 3/3 for just 4 mana. That’s already incredible, and you should play it in every green deck. Now, what can we do with its other ability? There are a lot of different tokens in this set, such as the 1/1 Officer s, 2/1 Klingon s, and Treasure s, any of which you can choose to upgrade into 3/3s if you have this card in play. This has the potential to be an absolute must-kill, and there are so many combos with it that it’ll just take a little bit of creativity to break wide open.

name: Hologram Stalker
prose: If you were looking for a good payoff for the black/green archetype, look no further than Hologram Stalker . Six mana gets you a good card out of your graveyard, a 2/2, and a 3/3. Incredible! Then, anything else you get out of the graveyard later creates another 3/3. I call this a payoff for black/green, but it’s honestly so strong on rate that every green deck should play it, and it’s likely the best green uncommon in Star Trek .

name: I'm a Doctor, Not a . . .
prose: It’s great to see another of McCoy’s favorite phrases immortalized on a card like this, but sadly, the card just isn’t very good. It may leave a +1/+1 counter behind, but I'm a Doctor, Not a . . . is still a very mediocre combat trick that I’m not going to want to play very often.

name: Jadzia Dax, Living Legacy
prose: One of Deep Space Nine ’s main characters, Jadzia Dax, Living Legacy is doing a pretty fair impression of a Badgermole Cub . While nowhere near as broken, Jadzia still sits back and creates large amounts of extra green mana for you. You can even use other cards to put +1/+1 counters on it and speed up the process. If you cast Dax on turn 2, it lets you play a 4-drop the following turn and then a 6-drop the turn after. Most mana dorks don’t do that. Plus, if you draw Dax late and it’s now bad to play, use it as a combat trick instead! A pretty solid card all round.

name: Jake Sisko, War Correspondent
prose: Eumidian Terrabotanist is already a fine card, so throw in the ability to investigate sometimes and you have a very nice card. There are a couple ways to enable that second land drop naturally, and you’ll be very happy if Jake Sisko, War Correspondent is able to turn the odd ramp spell into extra Clue tokens.

name: MACO Strike Team
prose: I’m sure that MACO Strike Team is going to be incredibly annoying in Constructed, but it seems a bit underpowered for Limited. The fact that it triggers from any of your creatures being targeted is fantastic, but as a 2/1 creature itself, it’s extremely weak and vulnerable. It’ll trade off in combat for no value and often won’t even be able to attack.

name: Moopsy
prose: I get to say this in every set review, but 1-mana 1/1s with deathtouch are really good. Yet none of them have ever been called Moopsy before, which honestly might be worth an extra point on the grade.

name: Mugato
prose: I’m not normally in the habit of giving praise to what’s basically a big vanilla creature, but reach and vigilance is such a deadly combination that I think Mugato is actually better than it looks. It’s so hot right now!

name: Neelix, Moral Support
prose: Neelix might be one of the most disliked characters in all of Star Trek ; he’s just kind of annoying and often used as comic relief despite none of the jokes really landing. There’s nothing wrong with Neelix, Moral Support in theory, but aside from the Food token it gives you, there aren’t very many sources of lifegain to help it trigger repeatedly.

name: Photosynthetic Physician
prose: A 5/5 reach creature for 5 mana is alright, but not exciting. What I actually like about Photosynthetic Physician is its graveyard ability, so I’d rather mill or discard it and then have it leave the graveyard for some value and hopefully trigger one of the green/black payoffs for doing so.

name: Rok-Tahk, Budding Scientist
prose: I really don’t get this card. Even at 4 or 5 mana, I don’t think it’d be good, so at 6 mana I’m baffled. Rok-Tahk, Budding Scientist is simply over-costed and doesn’t do something that a 6-drop wants to do. The indestructible Murf token is kind of interesting, but it’s such a weird reward for casting a 6-mana beater.

name: Saru, Unthreatened
prose: As the moral compass of the U.S.S. Discovery , whenever Michael Burnham strays, Saru is there to set her back on course. Therefore, it’s very appropriate to see Saru, Unthreatened as a creature who saves another creature from danger. Being a 3/2 itself is also a really nice rate for its mana cost, so I’d play Saru in basically any green deck.

name: Saurian Explorer
prose: Landfall decks typically suffer from running out of lands and not being able to trigger their abilities anymore. Not only does Saurian Explorer attack as a 6/5 when you can trigger it, or even an 8/7 or 10/9, but its activated ability gives you a guaranteed way to trigger landfall in the late game, which I’m sure the landfall decks are going to want.

name: Species 8472
prose: The trouble with playing any 6-drop is the massive loss of tempo you’ll feel if your opponent is able to remove it as soon as it hits the board. But if your 6-drop gains a bunch of life when it enters, that helps to offset that tempo loss. Species 8472 does exactly that, and it might even gain as much as 5 or 6 life in a good Strange New Worlds deck. This is exactly the sort of big thing I’d want to ramp into in that deck.

name: Stable Wormhole
prose: Stable Wormhole isn’t a card I’d want to put in an average green deck. On balance, it’s likely just worse than Final Frontier . However, the landfall deck in particular is an aggressive one that really wants to hit more land drops, and this does seem like a good way to enable that turn after turn. That seems like a deck that could utilize this to great effect, but I wouldn’t want it anywhere else.

name: Support Mission
prose: I hate playing cards like this. Support Mission does nothing to affect the board on the turn you play it, and that’s the key problem here. While all the mission cards in this cycle have that drawback, they all make up for it by having considerably better effects than this does. This simply feels like something you should leave in the sideboard and move on.

name: Sylvia Tilly, Joy of Discovery
prose: Tilly was, by far, my favorite character in Discovery . She was so sweet and pure, and her struggles with anxiety and self-doubt were inspiring to me at a difficult time in my life. Her card, Sylvia Tilly, Joy of Discovery , has a few things going on. It’s primarily a payoff for the graveyard deck. Tilly can theoretically give you a +1/+1 counter each turn, but I feel like you won’t be able to fill your graveyard often enough to fuel that for too long. Instead, it gives a nice bit of value when it enters, and then triggers your black/green cards when you need it to. Can’t ask for much more than that.

name: Syndicate Liquidators
prose: Giving two +1/+1 counters to any target creature is a really nasty effect to have on this creature. While Syndicate Liquidators is an obvious home for them since it has trample, it’ll often be better to spread the love and put the counters elsewhere, since this will already be a prime target for your opponent’s removal spells. What scares me most is that we’ve seen several ways to get multiple land drops in a turn, so I could definitely see a turn when Syndicate Liquidators grows from a 4/4 to a 10/10 and just goes to town.

name: Temporal Conqueror
prose: We’ve seen this exact card in previous sets between Temporal Conqueror , Eccentric Farmer , and Ostrich-Horse , which all varied in power level. In Star Trek , getting the land back from your graveyard triggers gravebreak effects, allowing it to be an even better card later in the game. Temporal Conqueror is definitely going to appear on my shortlist for best green common in the set.

name: Test of Courage
prose: While I think artifact removal is worth main-decking in TRK, one as restrictive as this doesn’t seem good enough. Test of Courage feels like a solid sideboard card and nothing more.

name: U.S.S. Discovery, at Black Alert
prose: When designing the card, U.S.S. Discovery, the Black Alert , of course the discover mechanic made sense to use. Getting to discover 5 when Discovery enters or attacks is huge, and it’s even one of the easier spacecraft to station! I don’t think anyone’s beating this card too frequently, it’s just such a beating to get buried in card advantage this way.

name: U.S.S. Voyager, Lone Wanderer
prose: The classic U.S.S. Voyager, Lone Wanderer of course has to do with lands. The Voyager crew became the first in Starfleet to explore the uncharted Delta Quadrant on their way home to Earth. We normally see some variants on Explosive Vegetation in sets these days, so seeing it attached to a spacecraft makes me think this one will be very strong. This is of course best suited for Landfall or Strange New Worlds decks, but it’s strong enough to see play elsewhere if you need it to.

name: Warp Speed
prose: At first glance, Warp Speed seems like it’s doing a lot. It fetches you a land , it guarantees your lands all enter play untapped, and it can turn itself into two extra cards in the late game. The problem is that it costs 3 mana to not affect the board and to not accelerate your mana, and that is not good. I could be wrong about this, but I think there are far better ways to enable strange new worlds in this set and this, sadly, won’t be good enough.

name: Xenobotanist
prose: Yep, a 2-drop mana dork in green . Xenobotanist is a great card. It fixes your mana, and you should take it very highly.

name: Xindi Surveyors
prose: I’d call this virtually unplayable in many sets. But in Star Trek , landfall is surprisingly well supported. A turn-3 Xindi Surveyors might end up a 6/5 on turn 4, so I could definitely see this being playable in that deck. But I wouldn’t want to play it elsewhere.

name: All Good Things...
prose: Perhaps not the episode I’d have chosen here. All Good Things. . . was The Next Generation ’s final episode. It sees Picard, tasked by Q, attempting to solve the mystery of a spatial anomaly from three distinct points in time simultaneously. This naturally gives way to a saga that does the same thing three times and culminates in a final ability. Just like the name suggests, this saga gives you “all good things”. Five mana to draw six cards and exile three is a pretty good deal. The 10 life is definitely not irrelevant either, and it gives you a big incentive for exiling three lands if you can. This looks like a good draw spell if you can enable it, and it might even be worth splashing.

name: Borg Cube
prose: One of the things that made the Borg so distinctive was the intimidating design of their ships. They were simply massive cubes or spheres floating through space, and seemingly impossible to penetrate. Borg Cube looks obscenely powerful. If you’ve built a strong black/white deck, the affinity should bring its cost down to around 3 or 4 mana, so you can use it as a removal spell. Stationing it may prove difficult, but your reward if you do so is the ability to assimilate the creature you removed in the first place. I’m hesitant to give this a flat 10/10 due to its high costs, but this looks like one of the scariest cards to play against.

name: The City on the Edge of Forever
prose: Widely regarded as the best episode of the original series, and I’m inclined to agree, The City on the Edge of Forever sees a deranged McCoy time travel back to the 1930s and inadvertently alter the present so that Starfleet never existed. As Kirk and Spock chase after him, they meet Edith Keeler, and from there a moral dilemma unfolds that you really have to see for yourself. It really is incredible. Anyway, the card tells this story excellently, and it provides enough value that it looks like it should be worth playing.

name: Cleveland Booker, Empath
prose: Even if they can’t block, creating a free 2/2 token on landfall is an incredibly powerful ability. Especially considering the fact that there are many ways to give yourself additional land drops each turn. Cleveland Booker, Empath looks perfectly suited to any aggressive landfall deck, but the “can’t block” clause on these tokens likely prices it out of being included in other decks for value.

name: Constable Odo
prose: The ability I like the most on Constable Odo is naturally the double investigate. Two Clue s is the easiest way to turn Odo into card advantage, but having a nice tempo play by stunning a creature for a few turns is certainly going to come up from time to time, too.

name: Dal R'El, Augment Orphan
prose: Having seen just how aggressive the landfall deck appears to be, this card disappoints me. With all of its extra lands, this deck shouldn’t have much trouble with mana, and Dal R'El, Augment Orphan does virtually nothing to advance the aggressive game plan. This card isn’t bad, but it’s not a gold card I’d look to pick up early.

name: Daniels, Temporal Agent
prose: You had me at Gravedigger . Daniels, Temporal Agent is a powerful two-for-one play that should be in any deck that can feasibly cast it, plain and simple. In black/green specifically, its second ability gives Daniels a built-in way to leave the graveyard and trigger all of your payoffs for a second time. This card is awesome and so clean. Pick it early, and often.

name: Dathon, His Heart Open
prose: Darmok is a work of art. The Tamarian language and culture is all based around telling stories. In one of the best scenes of the episode, Darmok signals to Picard that he’d like to hear a story from Earth, so Picard tells him the story of Gilgamesh and Enkidu. Sadly, Dathon is injured and doesn’t survive the night. Dathon, His Heart Open is naturally a card that works with sagas. There are 10 of them in Star Trek , so Dathon can do some things, but I don’t know if this will come together in Limited.

name: The Doctor, EMH
prose: At the bare minimum, The Doctor, EMH represents a 3/3 and two +1/+1 counters for 5 mana, which is exactly what I’d expect for that mana cost. If you have any other +1/+1 counters in play though, you can get so much more out of it. The Doctor can always put its counter on itself to maximize the number of counters you can get, and if it ends up putting four or more counters on board, that mana cost starts to look like a bargain.

name: The Duras Sisters
prose: A 3/2 with a very good death trigger for just 2 mana is really good. Better yet, having a hybrid mana cost means that you’ll never fail to cast The Duras Sisters on turn 2 in a black/red Klingons deck. This is just the perfect aggressive 2-drop for that deck, and something I’d prioritize early.

name: D'Vana Tendi, Optimistic Ensign
prose: While 3-drop mana dorks aren’t the greatest, D'Vana Tendi, Optimistic Ensign gives you something good to spend your extra mana on. I’d happily play this in any blue/green deck, but I’d fear that the double color pips in its cost might hinder its playability in a deck that’s only one of its colors.

name: Gowron, Eager for Battle
prose: As you’d expect from a rare, multicolored Klingon in this set, Gowron, Eager for Battle is the perfect sacrifice outlet for the deck. By sacrificing a Klingon to Gowron, it gets a +1/+1 counter, trample, and you draw a card. That’s a great deal, and we’ve already seen several Klingons that wouldn’t mind dying a glorious death in battle to galvanize their leader.

name: Gray and Adira, Forever Joined
prose: The trouble with cards like this is that while it’s supposed to be a payoff for a noncreature spells deck, it requires you to have creatures to use it with. Cards like that have historically not been good. Don’t get me wrong, there are some great creatures that you could combine with Gray and Adira, Forever Joined , but you’ll need those to justify this card. At the very least it can copy itself so you’ll always get another 2/3 to attack with.

name: Hemmer, Fixing What Is Broken
prose: I was frankly hoping for more out of the signpost uncommon for spacecraft. Perhaps even a powerful spacecraft? Hexproof is a cool ability to give, but Hemmer, Fixing What Is Broken isn’t an exciting enough payoff to move in on this color pair. This is clearly worth playing, but I doubt I’d even miss it if my white/blue deck failed to find one.

name: Hit It!
prose: Giving all your creatures haste definitely isn’t worth playing a whole card for, so the power of Hit It! has to rely on its other ability. I really dislike how it’s only very likely to ramp you and not simply guaranteed. I just know that small percentage chance will come back to bite me often enough to hate this card. I’ll play it and it’ll probably work, but I won’t be all that happy about it.

name: The Inner Light
prose: Another of The Next Generation ’s greatest episodes, The Inner Light sees the Enterprise encounter a probe in deep space that forces Picard to live out a lifetime as a member of a long dead alien race. It’s a beautiful story, and it makes for a very powerful saga. Reanimating a creature and then potentially drawing a bunch of cards is well worth the mana cost here, and it doesn’t take much to support it.

name: Kira Nerys, Firebrand
prose: Kira Nerys, Firebrand is a very unique and interesting design. While it looks powerful for certain Constructed decks, I can’t think of all that many ways to utilize Kira in Limited, mostly just flash creatures or instant-speed token-makers. As a 4/3 trampler for 3 mana, it’s obviously playable, but that might end up being all Kira can be in most cases.

name: Kirk, Commanding Officer
prose: We’ve not seen a lot of good reasons to care about getting to 8 power’s worth of creatures, despite it being the red/white mechanic. Kirk, Commanding Officer is a good reason though. Impulse drawing a card when you attack, no matter whether Kirk itself attacks, is really powerful and also something you can repeat turn after turn. This red/white deck doesn’t look very promising, but Kirk at least is something worth building around.

name: Live Long and Prosper
prose: You can clearly see what they were trying to do with this card. Doubling your life total means to live long and doubling the cards in your hand means to prosper. I get it, but what if your life total is low and you have no cards in hand? It’s almost like saying you can only Live Long and Prosper if you’re already prosperous and healthy, and that’s not something I can get on board with.

name: Locutus, the One Who Speaks
prose: In one of The Next Generation ’s best plot twists, the season three finale sees the Borg assimilate Picard into their collective, giving him new life as “Locutus”. Locutus, the One Who Speaks is an incredibly powerful Borg payoff, giving +1/+1 to all your artifact creatures, including itself. If that doesn’t take your fancy, Locutus is also a removal spell that you can use from your hand. This card is awesome and one of the reasons I’m excited to build a Borg deck in Limited.

name: Lore, Positronic Provocateur
prose: Lore was essentially Data’s “evil twin brother” and a recurring villain in The Next Generation . Lore, Positronic Provocateur isn’t quite as exciting as the character might have you believe. Both abilities are solid, but not exciting. Given that Lore makes you face a dilemma, it has a clear home in your blue/black decks, but it’s likely not good enough to see play in many other builds.

name: L'Rell, Fierce Visionary
prose: Sacrifice decks are always going to want access to as much sacrifice fodder as you can give them. L'Rell, Fierce Visionary is perfect for providing you with an endless stream of Klingon tokens to sacrifice, which should then pair well with the sacrifice payoffs we’ve seen.

name: Mirror Universe Intrusion
prose: Creating a permanent clone of a creature is one thing, but to have that restricted to only creatures your opponent controls is worrying. Mirror Universe Intrusion has the potential to be a back-breaking card, but if your opponent controls no creatures or only weak ones, it does next to nothing. I might be too harsh with this one, but I don’t like it when cards have big downsides like this.

name: Nog, Ambitious Cadet
prose: On its own, Nog, Ambitious Cadet can attack as a 3/4 with menace on turn 3 and immediately surveil. From there, if you level it up to its final ability, Nog can easily give you a bunch of free land drops, which also give you the added benefit of having cards leave your graveyard. This is a neat little package that looks unassuming at first but could add up to a significant advantage in a very short span of time.

name: Phlox, Unorthodox Doctor
prose: I do love to draw some cards as a reward for doing what an archetype wants, but Phlox, Unorthodox Doctor isn’t quite that simple. Having your creature deal combat damage to a player as well as have a counter on it means there are two ways in which this could go wrong. Phlox is certainly powerful, but you do need to put in a bit of extra work to make it pop off. Keep in mind that this automatically works with spacecraft, since they’ll have charge counters on them when they’re attacking.

name: Sarek, Federation Ambassador
prose: Sarek was a recurring character in multiple Star Trek projects as both Vulcan’s ambassador to Earth and Spock’s father. Sarek, Federation Ambassador simply asks you to control five or more creature types to draw a card. Given that most creatures in this set have two creature types and there’s very little overlap, this effectively means you need three creatures in play, including Sarek. That sounds very strong, and it also scales extremely well if you can theoretically get up to 10 types.

name: Seven of Nine
prose: You can’t ask for much more than drawing a card whenever you face a dilemma. We know from past experiences that this is among the best kinds of payoff for a Draft archetype, and dilemmas are extremely well supported in Star Trek. Seven of Nine is an excellent build-around for blue/black.

name: Spock, Always Your Friend
prose: We’ve seen a lot of creatures similar to this in the past, like Augur of Bolas or Wandering Mind . They’re typically very good, and Spock, Always Your Friend isn’t only a good rate for this, but also lets you pick up artifacts and enchantments, giving you a much wider range of available options. Spock is an excellent enabler for this blue/red deck and also one of the best creatures we’ve seen to pair with beam me up spells.

name: The Traveler
prose: I really hoped for more out of the blue/green signpost uncommon. The Traveler has the potential to have a lot of power, but that 3 toughness means you’ll find it difficult to put that power to use, as it trades off with anything that has 3 power of its own. This card is definitely playable, but I really wanted something more interesting.

name: Vash, Freelance Archaeologist
prose: I think the archetype that impresses me the most in terms of payoffs is the black/green one. We’ve seen several good ways to have things leave your graveyard for profit, and Vash, Freelance Archaeologist is just another great reward for that. There’s not much else to say. This archetype looks cool, and Vash is excellent in it.

name: Worf, Honor-Bound Warrior
prose: I’m sure Worf would be the one to tell you that a warrior is patient and waits for the right moment to strike. Worf, Honor-Bound Warrior is perfect for sitting back, building up counters, and then striking when it’s big enough to attack profitably into your opponent’s blockers. This Worf doesn’t even need to attack to look threatening, and your opponent will likely need to deal with it at some point, which is a big compliment for a 2-drop 1/1.

name: Year of Hell
prose: Certainly my favorite episode of Voyager , this two-parter sees Janeway and the crew navigating through the space of a hostile race with temporal manipulating weapons for an entire year. These people have used their weapons to erase entire enemy races from history, and now they’re trying to do the same to Voyager . Over the Year of Hell , Voyager loses countless fights and falls further and further into disrepair as you see the strain this puts on the whole crew. It’s an epic spectacle, but apparently not epic enough to make a remotely playable saga out of it.

name: Zero, Incorporeal Sensate
prose: As far as annoying little artifact creatures go, Zero, Incorporeal Sensate is certainly up there. It’s essentially an uncommon Elite Spellbinder that also works with all of your Borg payoffs, despite not being a Borg itself. This kind of disruption won’t do a lot, but it might force an opponent to switch plans or not commit a powerful card to the board when they wanted to, which is more than enough to warrant playing this card.

name: Class-F Shuttlecraft
prose: We keep getting sets where the generic 3-drop mana rock is actually playable, and I believe this one is too. Class-F Shuttlecraft can fix your mana in any deck you want, but it also gives you the upside of getting to attack later in the game. It doesn’t do a ton, but it certainly gets the job done.

name: Combadge
prose: I get the gimmick, I really do, but Combadge feels embarrassingly bad. You have to pay 3 mana to cast it, and then spend 4 mana equipping both copies to your creatures to make them both unblockable . Except that disrupting one of them disrupts the other. Your opponent could even remove one of the communicators, and then the other one does absolutely nothing. This feels like a big miss to me.

name: Crystalline Entity
prose: The Crystalline Entity was an early “villain” in The Next Generation , an all-powerful entity that the Enterprise crew couldn’t figure out how to stop. It was highly destructive, so seeing it here as a massive creature that wipes the board when it enters seems very appropriate. It’s worth accelerating into, and you can play it in any deck willing to do that, which makes it sound like an incredible bomb.

name: Cybernetic Specialist
prose: Cybernetic Specialist is quite unassuming. It’s a strictly better version of Sanitation Automaton from Murders at Karlov Manor , which was a huge overperformer. It has synergy in white-black and green-black, and might be a perfectly fine curve-filler for just about any deck.

name: Deep Space 9
prose: Well then. The titular space station of its own show, Deep Space 9 looks like one hell of a big win condition. Potentially four entirely free permanents every single turn is absolutely incredible, and it even spots you the first four as soon as it enters. And that’s not to say anything about stationing it and giving a massive +3/+3 to all your creatures. DS9 is almost guaranteed to win you the game if you get to play it, the only problem is finding a way to cast a 9-drop, but I’m definitely up for the challenge.

name: Engineered Explosives
prose: Engineered Explosives is a classic Magic card that has been a competitive mainstay for over 20 years. If you have access to more than just two colors, it allows you to destroy just about anything your opponent might put in front of you, which is incredibly flexible for an otherwise colorless removal spell . It’s a bit expensive to use, but that flexibility can’t be beaten.

name: The Holodeck
prose: The Holodeck was probably one the coolest innovations for The Next Generation as it allowed the writers to tell a greater range of stories in the series. The card is extremely powerful, especially as it always allows you to play any basic land from outside the game , and the permanents you get from your graveyard can keep recurring themselves. The problem is simply being able to take a turn off to play a 7-drop that does nothing the turn you play it. That’s an extremely hefty cost, and one that I’m not sure we’ll even be able to pay.

name: Isolinear Processor
prose: We don’t get a lot of 2-drop mana rocks for a very good reason; they’re usually too strong. Isolinear Processor may only be restricted to playing artifacts, but there are a lot of good ones to ramp into, and this can be a good way to enable some of the more powerful artifacts in Star Trek .

name: Replicator
prose: I’ve been playing Pauper a bit recently and am learning how powerful Campfire can be, simply because it’s a cheap artifact that sits in play and gains you life every turn. Replicator has a lot of that same energy going on, as you can just copy the Food token it gives you every turn and use them to stay alive. On top of that, this set has quite a few Clue tokens and 1/1s lying around for you to copy, so I’d imagine it shouldn’t be too difficult to use Replicator every turn for something good.

name: Sickbay
prose: Five mana is a lot for this effect, maybe too much. Sickbay at least gives you a +1/+1 counter on the turn you play it and then gives you two counters on any turn in which you played a creature. Food tokens turn into three additional counters, and playing the planet duals also rewards you with extra counters. There’s a lot to like about where all of this is going, but I just wonder if 5 mana is too much to enable it all.

name: Tea, Earl Grey, Hot
prose: Captain Picard’s go-to drink is well known among Trekkies. Tea, Earl Grey, Hot are words uttered in countless episodes of TNG. The card is really good too, you’re probably always happy with a 2-mana artifact that draws a card in any deck that cares about noncreature spells or artifacts.

name: Tricorder
prose: Short Sword variants crop up time and time again, and they’re usually only slightly outside the realm of what’s playable. I believe Tricorder gives you enough upside on top of your usual +1/+1 to play this in a few decks, though I’d also cut it from plenty of others.

name: Type-2 Phaser
prose: I’m not sure we’ll be setting our phasers to stun any time soon. While it’s cool that this stuns a creature when it enters, I can’t help but be put off by that expensive equip cost. Type-2 Phaser does some good things, but 3 to equip when it doesn’t give any boosts to toughness feels a bit too much.

name: U.S.S. Cerritos, Following Up
prose: I laughed at S.H.I.E.L.D. Helicarrier and called it unplayable. Players were so desperate for flying creatures in Marvel Super Heroes that it actually performed fine, but I still maintain that it was awful. U.S.S. Cerritos, Following Up looks almost identical to that, but it’s a spacecraft rather than a vehicle , which to me makes all the difference. You get your officers up front when you play it, and it shouldn’t take too long for you to find the 6 counters you need to get it running.

name: U.S.S. Enterprise-D, Galaxy-Class
prose: The legendary ship captained by Jean-Luc Picard, the U.S.S. Enterprise-D, Galaxy-Class is one of the more powerful spacecraft in this set. It essentially gives you an impulse draw the first time you station it in a turn, which is something you can easily control. If you play it right, you can get a ton of free card advantage from this one card. Better yet, you can keep stationing it even after it becomes a creature and keep the card advantage flowing. The Enterprise-D is a phenomenal card and probably one of the strongest first picks in the entire set, given that any deck can play it.

name: Warp Core
prose: Using Warp Core to find a basic land makes it playable in a lot of different decks. I’m intrigued by its ability to station your spacecraft though, as doing so with any excess mana you have will take a lot of pressure away from your creatures. This is an interesting card for sure, and one that might play a pivotal role within the set.

name: Vulcan
prose: Like in any set, dual lands are important for fixing your mana and enabling splashes. These planets can do a little extra as they’re searchable by some cards in TRK and provide additional names towards strange new worlds abilities. You should typically pick these over mediocre commons for your deck, but not over more premium ones, though this dynamic can also shift if there are splash colors that you’re looking to fix for.

name: Temporal Anomaly
prose: These utility lands are pretty interesting as far as cycles go. They’re remarkably similar to the “blighted” lands from Battle for Zendikar , but sacrificing them doesn’t put you down on lands. Colorless lands do come with a hefty cost because they don’t fix your colors, but I think you should be able to afford the occasional copy in a 2-color deck, given that their abilities are all quite strong.

name: Watery Grave
prose: They may be some of the strongest dual lands in Magic, but in Limited the shock lands aren’t much different from any other dual land. They’ll be great for fixing your colors and for enabling strange new worlds, but that’s about as far as it goes.

name: The Unicomplex
prose: Each of these lands provides you with what should be a strict upgrade over a basic land of the same color, with a very minor bonus when they enter. They each surveil 1, which we know from past experiences is a very good thing to do for free, and the additional modes that they have are also quite interesting, especially on The Unicomplex . You should generally take these a little higher in your pick order than a random dual land, but still not over premium spells for your deck.

name: Starfleet Academy
prose: For Starfleet Academy to net you any mana, you need to have at least seven different creature types in play. While that’s not impossible, it doesn’t sound very likely at all, and even when that happens you’d need mana sinks to make it matter. This looks completely unplayable to me, and harder to enable than similar lands of the past that were also useless in Limited.

name: Unexplored Territory
prose: While you get access to some mana on the turn you play it, on balance Unexplored Territory is simply worse than an Evolving Wilds , which we have a precedent for in how poor Shire Terrace was in The Lord of the Rings . That’s not to say it’s bad or unplayable, but it doesn’t feel like the easy slam dunk that it could be. Still, it’s good enough for fixing both your mana and your strange new worlds count, so picking one up probably won’t hurt.

name: Mikaeus, the Lunarch
prose: Mikaeus, the Lunarch was an absolute bomb when it was first printed 15 years ago. Nowadays, power creep has settled in a little bit. This feels a fair bit worse than Reality Fracture ’s Guiding Hydra , though it’s still strong enough that you should always play it in a white deck.

name: Flare of Fortitude
prose: While casting this for no mana is quite interesting, the effect isn’t. Flare of Fortitude isn’t something you should put in your deck, no matter how you end up casting it.

name: Kenrith, the Returned King
prose: No matter which colors you have in your deck, Kenrith, the Returned King should be powerful. Its abilities are expensive, but beyond the red one, any one of them can win you the game if you activate it over and over.

name: Sisay, Weatherlight Captain
prose: If you’re able to activate the ability of Sisay, Weatherlight Captain , it can definitely be very powerful. But all five colors is a big ask, so I don’t think it’s very likely to happen. The Strange New Worlds archetype might be able to make this work, but it’s a long shot at best. The sheer number of legends, especially hybrid ones, might actually get Sisay up to a 4/4 or 5/5.

name: Thada Adel, Acquisitor
prose: Blue decks in TRK Limited are bound to have a few artifacts in them, so Thada Adel, Acquisitor is likely to be an unblockable 2/2 that rips apart your opponent’s deck, potentially giving you a bunch of free cards too. Against nonblue decks, you’ll have to find a way to make it unblockable, but about a quarter of the cards in Star Trek are artifacts, so you’re bound to find some good stuff to steal.

name: Empress Galina
prose: When Empress Galina was first printed, there were very few legendary permanents in the game. You might have 10 or so in a set to help tell the story. But in a Universes Beyond set, that number is very different. There are 104 legendary permanent cards in Star Trek , and Galina can steal each and every one of them. Yes, you have to untap with it and it adds almost nothing to the board by itself, but once you steal even one creature, you stand to win the game off Empress Sato’s back.

name: Arcum Dagsson
prose: Since there are some expensive noncreature artifacts in TRK that we’d really like to cheat out , such as The Holodeck and Deep Space 9 , I could see Arcum Dagsson playing a role every now and again. However, in a vast majority of cases, turning your creatures into noncreatures isn’t something you can afford to do in Limited. This is a big miss.

name: Bruvac the Grandiloquent
prose: I absolutely love Bruvac the Grandiloquent . It’s in fact my main commander. But there are literally zero cards in this set that combine with it. Unless you really want to play Zachary Quinto as a Horned Turtle , you should never play this.

name: Decree of Pain
prose: For all its different reprints, we’ve not actually seen Decree of Pain in a 1v1 Draft set since it was first printed in Scourge back in 2003. I’m not often in the habit of casting 8-mana spells, but a board wipe that draws a bunch of cards sounds very appealing. This is something I’d want to take early and then make sure I had the mana acceleration to hit it often. It’s also fantastic if you cycle it, so you can’t really go wrong.

name: Drivnod, Carnage Dominus
prose: There are a few death triggers in this set, but Drivnod, Carnage Dominus doing barely anything else isn’t a great look. At 3 toughness, it really needs that indestructible counter to survive and even then, there are still plenty of ways to answer it. I could see it doing some work in the right deck, but a lot has to go right before I’d feel happy about it.

name: Sheoldred, the Apocalypse
prose: I have… thoughts about this. Benedict Cumberbatch aside, Sheoldred, the Apocalypse is an unbelievably powerful card. While it provides no card advantage whatsoever and might simply die to removal, the simple fact that it punishes your opponent for trying to find that removal is the most crippling part about it. All the while, nothing can get into combat with it, and you get to buffer your own life total. Sheoldred is a menace and likely one of the best cards in this set.

name: Torbran, Thane of Red Fell
prose: The triple red on Torbran, Thane of Red Fell is definitely a downside, but the effect you get is incredibly powerful. I especially like how this will buff the damage from both the 1/1 Officer tokens and the 2/1 Klingon tokens. Just be aware that you may want to skew your mana base a little to help accommodate for its cost.

name: Loot, Exuberant Explorer
prose: Loot, Exuberant Explorer isn’t bad by any means, but it does almost nothing in the early game. A 1/4 is an okay blocker, but you’re not guaranteed to have enough lands to make use of extra land drops. Late game however, just activating it each turn provides you with free value, so it definitely gets better as you approach the end of the game and need to find a way to win.

name: Rishkar, Peema Renegade
prose: All the value you get from Rishkar, Peema Renegade is given to you upfront. You don’t need to wait around; you just immediately get your two +1/+1 counters, one probably going on Keenser and the other on your 2-drop. That’s simply excellent, and it gives you quite a sizable early lead in any game in which you play it.

name: Bristly Bill, Spine Sower
prose: I just want to say that representing McCoy as Bristly Bill, Spine Sower is a stroke of genius. Also, Bristly Bill is a spectacular card. Putting a +1/+1 counter on something with every land you play is incredible, and in the late game, its activated ability is often better than using your mana to cast a new spell. It’s a must-kill threat, and if you play this early enough, it takes over the game. Excellent card!

name: Sen Triplets
prose: Sen Triplets is, as I understand it, a much-maligned commander. Getting to play cards from an opponent’s hand in a 4-player game can be pretty nasty. In 1v1 Limited, it’s just not as good. I can definitely see the potential, but a 3-color card that does nothing until the turn after you’ve played it doesn’t sound very good to me.

name: Tatyova, Benthic Druid
prose: Tatyova, Benthic Druid is one of my favorite “mythic uncommons” of the past. The fact that it draws you a card every time you play a land means you naturally draw into more lands and can keep triggering it every turn. Tatyova was a big disappointment when it returned in Foundations , but this set’s architecture is built around lands so much more.

name: Hull Breach
prose: I think it’s worth main-decking artifact removal in Star Trek , and Hull Breach is certainly good enough for that. If you manage to catch a strong enchantment at the same time, then all the better.

name: Isshin, Two Heavens as One
prose: Isshin, Two Heavens as One is a difficult card to get right. In the context of this set, you’re mostly looking at the attack triggers from cards in the red/white archetype, but splashing black in an aggressive Boros deck might not be possible. I’d love to see it happen, but I don’t think it will.

name: Ertai Resurrected
prose: Even though each ability lets your opponent draw a card, it’s hard to feel too scared of anything your opponent might do if you sit back with an Ertai Resurrected in your hand. Countering or destroying anything at instant speed and putting a 3/2 onto the board is phenomenal. It’s as simple as that.

name: Jhoira, Weatherlight Captain
prose: In case you’re unaware, a “historic” spell is any artifact, saga, or legendary spell. Jhoira, Weatherlight Captain is pretty good, allowing you to draw a lot of free cards if you have a deck that can support it, but being a Hill Giant in stats definitely holds it back a lot.

name: Captain Sisay
prose: Captain Sisay looks like it should be good in a set with so many legendary cards in it, but this card is just outdated and weak. Four mana for a 2/2 is very bad, and it doesn’t do anything until you get to untap with it. It’s a hard pass from me.

name: Riku of Many Paths
prose: When it was announced in the late 2000s that there would be a new Star Trek movie with a brand-new recasting of the original Enterprise crew, fans were understandably excited. Leonard Nimoy was then announced to be appearing in a cameo role, but his Spock ended up being a main character and integral to the plot of the film, which perhaps explains why William Shatner wasn’t invited…. Anyway, Riku of Many Paths only worked with plot cards in Outlaws of Thunder Junction , but in a set with as many modal spells as this one, it looks incredibly powerful!

name: Prosper, Tome-Bound
prose: Prosper, Tome-Bound is one of the most popular commanders in my local scene, and for pretty good reason. Having it sit there and effectively draw you an extra card every turn is very powerful. But not only that, your opponent simply can’t attack a lot of creatures into a 1/4 with deathtouch.

name: Stella Lee, Wild Card
prose: We’ve never had Stella Lee, Wild Card in a Draft set before, but it looks really good. Blue/red’s archetype is based around noncreature spells already, and there are a lot of cheap cantrips that help to enable this. Beam me up is especially good for helping you cast two spells in a turn, so I have no trouble believing this will be a bomb in the right deck. Try to grab a couple copies of Make It So to aim for an infinite combo.

name: Mogis, God of Slaughter
prose: If you can enable the devotion on Mogis, God of Slaughter , then it’s obviously very good. My main concern is that Star Trek is very much not set up to enable that.
